World.title: Trump allies are poised to weaken protections for historic sites — not just in D.C.
World.content:
Trump allies are poised to weaken protections for historic sites — not just in D.C.

toggle caption Jen Golbeck/AP

The Trump administration is eyeing a workaround for one of the procedural hurdles facing its proposed 250-foot arch: weakening federal oversight of all construction projects affecting historic sites.

Critics say that the move would not only clear a path for President Trump's controversial projects in D.C., but also endanger the preservation of historic and cultural places across the United States.

"Every American who has any place in their heart that is historic or culturally significant to them should be concerned about this attempt to gut historic preservation protections," said Greg Werkheiser, founding partner at the law firm Cultural Heritage Partners.

Sponsor Message

The National Register of Historic Places contains over 100,000 properties, encompassing more than 1.8 million buildings, structures, sites, objects and districts. They take many forms, from a house to a burial ground, a shipwreck to a landscape, a single tree to an entire neighborhood.

"It's the thing that defines America," Werkheiser said. "The places that you go where your family has an attachment over generations … There are millions of these sites in this country, and all of them are made less protected by this effort by the Trump administration."

The White House and the Department of the Interior did not respond to NPR's request for comment.

Part of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966, known as Section 106, requires federal agencies to evaluate how new construction projects would affect historic places.

Under the Section 106 review process, the federal agency overseeing a project must invite interested parties — like preservation groups and local and tribal governments — to weigh in. Currently, agencies are required to consider whether the project would cause "adverse effects" to a historic property and, if so, explore ways to "avoid, minimize, or mitigate" those harms.

The Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, the federal agency responsible for overseeing the Section 106 review process, is packed with Trump appointees. And now, 60 years after the law took effect, the council wants to water it down drastically.

Sponsor Message

"Because President Trump controls 21 of the 24 members of the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, it's very likely that they will proceed with doing what the administration wants for them to do," said Sara Bronin, who served as the Senate-confirmed chair of the advisory council under President Biden.

Bronin is the most recent chair of the council, as that position is currently vacant. President Trump has yet to nominate a new one, instead appointing its vice chair, Travis Voyles, to serve in an acting capacity.

Last week, Voyles sent an email to council members asking them to vote on proposed revisions to the wording of Section 106. According to draft language obtained by NPR, those changes include redefining what kinds of properties can be considered historic in the first place, making public comment on new projects optional and removing the requirement to consult with Native American tribes.

"What it means is that the federal government, in its own discretion, can decide whether — if ever — to tell an American community that it's about to do a major project that could harm or destroy a historic resource," Werkheiser said. "The public will be completely cut out of any conversation around the future of places that matter to them in this country."

Council members were given just one week to cast their votes, via email, by the end of Friday. The revision would need to clear several more steps of the federal rulemaking process, including a roughly 30-day public comment period, before it can take effect.

Werkheiser called the vote a "foregone conclusion," but said it sets the stage for a legal fight later.

"As sure as the sun rises and sets over Washington, D.C., there will be litigation in an attempt to stop this absurd gutting of protections of American history," he said.

toggle caption Scott Olson/Getty Images

Why does the Trump administration want these changes?

After World War II, an era of urban renewal and federal highway construction destroyed high-profile buildings like New York City's Penn Station, and devastated many historically Black neighborhoods.

Sponsor Message

The advisory council's memo describes that period as "one of the greatest, yet most destructive building streaks in American history." It prompted public outrage, and resulted in Congress passing the National Historic Preservation Act in 1966.

"Small wonder, then, that Congress enacted a requirement that all Federal agencies take into account historic preservation concerns in future Federal actions," the memo reads. "Consideration, however, was not the same thing as a mandate that historic preservation concerns trump all others."

The memo says the current regulations under Section 106 "create confusion and uncertainty for both the public and regulated entities and contribute to agency delays." It cites a 2019 study that found consultation can take nearly seven years in extreme cases.

And it proposes revisions that it says would help "agencies strike a more appropriate balance between evaluating effects on historic properties and advancing critical federal projects."

The changes would limit the type and number of historic properties that will receive protection, ruling out "significant landscape features" like the Grand Canyon. Bronin says it would also change the type of actions that will be reviewed in the first place, with an "alarming number of exemptions," including for federally funded projects carried out by local authorities.

"Things like state highway widening, which in the past have been highly destructive of historic places, including not only whole neighborhoods but also burial sites … won't [undergo Section 106 review] under the new rules," she said.

The new wording would also narrow what is considered an "adverse effect" to anything that is directly and foreseeably tied to the project (as opposed to indirect or cumulative effects). And it allows agencies to condense much of the process into a written report, which they would then share with third parties for review instead of consulting them along the way.

"This change in consultation will have the effect of not surfacing the location, significance and effects on historic sites, meaning that they could have the potential to be destroyed at scale," she said.

Sponsor Message

The new wording would also remove requirements for public comment, eliminating the phrase: "views of the public are essential to informed Federal decisionmaking."

That stands out to Charles Birnbaum, the founding president and CEO of The Cultural Landscape Foundation, an education and advocacy organization based in D.C. He told NPR over email that he sees similarities between the revised law and the reason it exists in the first place.

"Consent of the governed is being replaced with my way or the highway," he wrote. "This is the same haughty, retrograde, and myopic attitude that resulted in urban renewal, which decimated cities with highways and destroyed countless neighborhoods nationwide, especially underserved communities."

The Cultural Landscape Foundation has already sued over the administration's repainting of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, saying the National Park Service improperly used — by its own words — a "streamlined" Section 106 review. A judge has not yet ruled in the case, as the pool saga continues to unfold.

toggle caption Allison Robbert/AP

What happens next?

Simplifying the Section 106 review process could help to fast-track some of the Trump administration's renovation projects in D.C.

The requirement for third-party consultation — which many historic and cultural preservation groups say is happening too fast or not at all — has been one of the few hurdles in the already fast-moving approval process for Trump's arch.

Bronin says under the proposed new language, near-constant construction noise near Arlington National Cemetery would not be considered an adverse effect, and the 250-foot arch's disruption of historic views would not be considered under the review process.

"Although I would encourage listeners to not simply focus on D.C.'s iconic landmarks, because this proposal would have far-reaching effects, the proposal for the arch in front of Arlington Cemetery is an excellent example of what's at stake with these changes," Bronin said.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation, the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers and the National Conference of State Historic Preservation Officers have all issued statements opposing the Section 106 changes, taking issue both with the substance and the brief voting timeline. They each have representatives on the advisory council board.

Sponsor Message

Elizabeth Merrit, deputy general counsel for the National Trust for Historic Preservation, wrote in an open letter that she will vote against the proposed changes, calling them "likely to cause

widespread chaos and confusion, and … curtail the consultation process that has led to thousands of win-win outcomes around the country."

Werkheiser agreed that the proposal would be "terrible for developers," who want predictability and information early on to avoid delays and issues down the road. He said that's why the existing Section 106 process generally works so well. Trying to speed it up by even a few days, he said, would be "a losing trade for America in the long-term."

"Folks who complain about the relatively little time it takes to pause in front of a massive development project and say, 'Are we destroying something that can never be replaced?' I think those folks need to ask themselves, what legacy are they handing to their children and their grandchildren?" he said.

Both Werkheiser and Bronin encouraged people who oppose these changes to speak up not only during the public comment period, but to their legislators directly.

"As chair, I saw the topic of historic preservation as a bipartisan issue, and one that unites people who care about their communities, whether they're in red states or blue states," Bronin said. "I think that the public comment on the regulations will really help to send a powerful message that we care about our historic places and we don't want them to be destroyed."

Congress could potentially take action, including passing legislation to strengthen Section 106.

Democrats on the Senate Natural Resources Committee released a statement this week opposing the changes. They urged the council to "go back to the drawing board and work directly with Tribes and states on a new proposal that actually improves the consultation process without undermining the rights and voices of those most directly affected."

World.title: For a 2nd time, House approves resolution to end the war in Iran in a rebuke to Trump
World.content:
For a 2nd time, House approves resolution to end the war in Iran in a rebuke to Trump

toggle caption J. Scott Applewhite/AP

The House on Thursday approved a resolution to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran, in a vote that reflected growing frustration inside Congress over the war and the ability of lawmakers to conduct oversight.

The resolution passed the House by a vote of 214 to 208. And while it is not legally binding, the resolution represents a symbolic rebuke to President Trump over a war that lawmakers never voted to authorize. It was the second such rebuke passed by the House since the start of the war.

Shortly after the House vote, Senate Democrats tried to advance a war powers resolution of their own, but the measure failed 47 to 49.

Sponsor Message

The votes came at a moment when attacks between Iran and the U.S. appear to be intensifying. Eighteen U.S. troops have died since fighting broke out in February, but four have died since July 17. U.S. forces have also suffered nearly 500 injuries, with 100 of those coming in the past two weeks, according to the Pentagon.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., who led the effort in the House, said the vote sends President Trump a clear message that Congress will not continue to tolerate what she described as an "illegal war."

"From the beginning, this war has had no clear mission, no strategy, no end goal. Congress has not been consulted," Jayapal said following the vote. "And hostilities have been driven over and over again by a president who won his election by promising to end forever wars."

Four Republicans joined Democrats to approve the measure: Tom Barrett of Michigan, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Ohio's Warren Davidson and Thomas Massie of Kentucky.

Republicans who opposed the resolution have defended the war as necessary, given Iran's past attacks on Americans and U.S. interests in the region.

During debate on the House floor on Wednesday, the Republican chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Brian Mast of Florida, held up photos of U.S. service members killed in the war.

Sponsor Message

"To belittle this mission is to belittle and demean the very service these members gave their life for," Mast said. "This operation is bringing reckoning for the hundreds of times Iran has attacked and killed people of the United States of America," he continued.

Last month, the Senate also approved a war powers resolution, only to reverse course on a separate resolution brought the following day after President Trump criticized the initial vote. The president has referred to the war power votes as "meaningless" and a reflection of Democrats "fueled by Trump Derangement Syndrome."

World.title: Retaliation being considered if no deal reached by Trump's tariff deadline, Carney says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says 'everything is on the table,' including retaliation, if Canada can't reach a deal with the Trump administration before a U.S. deadline to impose new 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian exports.

Carney says retaliation on the table if Trump's new tariffs go ahead

Prime Minister Mark Carney says retaliatory measures are being considered if his government can't reach a deal with U.S. President Donald Trump before his new tariffs take effect.

"Everything is on the table depending on the outcome of the negotiations," Carney told reporters following a meeting with the 13 premiers in Charlottetown on Thursday.

Their face-to-face follows a threat from the White House to slap 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars' worth of Canadian imports come Aug. 19.

"If these tariffs or other measures come into force there's a full range of things that we can do," said Carney.

The prime minister wouldn't say what reprisals are in his back pocket, calling it "counterproductive" to talk retaliation with negotiations underway.

"But it's important to know what your options are," he said

WATCH | Carney on the 'opportunity' of the next few weeks: New tariff deadline 'creates an opportunity' to reach a comprehensive deal with U.S., Carney says | Duration 2:08 Asked whether the Aug. 19 tariff deadline is an opportunity to reach an end-game deal with the U.S. or a pressure tactic, Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'it's both.' Speaking at a press conference after meeting with Canada's premiers on Thursday, Carney said the U.S. has shown a level of engagement this week 'that reflects the seriousness of the trade relationship and the breadth of the issues.'

The agenda for meetings between the country's leaders this week in P.E.I. was upended on Monday when the White House announced the new tariffs, calling them a response to what it sees as Canadian discrimination against American motor vehicles, dairy and alcohol.

The new tariffs would hit over $20 billion of Canadian goods — including alcohol, electronics and hockey sticks — and is expected to hurt Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia the hardest.

Carney said he sees this latest deadline as a real opportunity to reach a trade deal — while also agreeing it's a classic Trump pressure tactic.

"It's both," he said. But "there's a level of engagement and breadth of engagement that reflects the seriousness of the trade relationship."

WATCH | Carney responds to U.S. tariffs: 'Whatever it takes': Carney on Canada's response to U.S. tariffs | Duration 1:01 Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada isn’t leaving anything off the table when it comes to dealing with the U.S.’s incoming 50 per cent tariffs on goods covered by a North American trade deal. Carney made the remarks at the First Minister’s Meeting in Charlottetown, where Canada’s premiers are gathering to discuss how to respond to U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats.

The question of retribution had been a pressure point during the provincial and territorial leaders' annual summer get-together.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford has been advocating for a more aggressive approach, including withholding Canada's potash and oil to "dismantle" the United States.

"It's very hard to deal with President Trump when he changes his mind every single day," said Ford.

"One day, the prime minister is with him side by side, and the next thing you know, President Trump turns on him like a rabid dog."

Oil as leverage 'a very dumb decision': Smith

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she doesn't support retaliatory tariffs, especially when it comes to oil.

"I'm going to try to prevent Canada from making a very dumb decision of putting energy on the table because Line 5 goes through Michigan," she told CBC's Power & Politics, referring to the pipeline that moves around 540,000 barrels per day of oil and natural gas across the Canada-U.S. border.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith crosses her fingers while speaking with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, centre, and New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt prior to meeting with Carney. (Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press)

"If you cut off energy to the United States, they can cut off Line 5 and cut off energy to Ontario and Quebec. So no aviation fuel, no diesel, no gasoline. And we don't want to do that," Smith said.

"I don't think you go into a negotiation promising to punch someone in the nose. You go into negotiation talking about a win-win."

Premiers insist on unity

Despite some disagreement emerging about how to negotiate, the premiers have been emphatic that they are united in a "Team Canada" approach to the trade war.

"Yeah, there's different opinions, but you need different opinions to come up with a solid strategy," said Northwest Territories Premiers R.J. Simpson after the meeting.

"I come out of there every time feeling very united. I think about the United States, they have nothing like this."

Stressing the unity theme, Carney didn't pass up an opportunity to use Charlottetown's history as the gathering spot for the Fathers of Confederation.

He noted that was a time when "trade barriers were holding back economic growth, major infrastructure projects increasingly required co-operation across jurisdictions and the threat of American invasion loomed large.

"Plus ça change," he said to the premiers. "What the Fathers of our Confederation suspected then, we know acutely today: that our unity is our greatest strength, and that our destiny is in our hands."

The premiers, in a joint communiqué Wednesday, urged the Carney government "to maintain a clear, timely consultation process with provinces and territories during negotiations."

World.title: Carney says he 'should have been clearer' about new Gordie Howe bridge agreement
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says he "imperfectly" described the new deal to open the Gordie Howe International Bridge after the text of the agreement appeared to contradict his original explanation.

While attending the Calgary Stampede shortly after the deal was struck — but before the text was made public — Carney told CTV that bridge toll revenue would only be split with the U.S. after accounting for operating costs, including repaying the debt.

But that suggestion seemed to contradict the text of the agreement, which was only made public late Tuesday and made no reference to Canada's debt.

When pressed about the contradiction during a news conference on Thursday, the prime minister said he "should have been clearer" in his original comments and that the new revenue-splitting deal with the U.S. doesn't account for debt repayment.

"Could I have explained it better on a Sunday morning at Stampede, with a cowboy hat on? Yes, I could have explained it better," he said.

The deal — described as a "proposed agreement in principle" — says that for the first 15 years, Canada will split half of the bridge's net revenue with an economic development fund "established and solely controlled" by the U.S. government.

WATCH | Carney on the new bridge deal: Carney says he could have explained new Gordie Howe bridge deal better | Duration 3:13 Prime Minister Mark Carney, when asked Thursday about previous remarks around revenue from the Gordie Howe bridge, attempted to clarify, saying an underlying deal between Canada and Michigan that states tolls won't be split until Ottawa's bridge-construction costs are repaid is still in place. But, he added, a more recent 'parallel' deal with the U.S. would see net revenues after expenses 'not including debt repayment' shared.

That new deal between Ottawa and Washington was reached even though Canada and Michigan struck an initial deal to build the bridge in 2012.

Under that original agreement, Canada fronted the money for the construction of the bridge — which came in at $6.4 billion — and Canada was set to collect the tolls until the cost was repaid, after which the revenues would be split with Michigan.

Carney said that his initial comments about debt repayment being included in the deal were meant to be a reference to the original agreement with Michigan — even though he referenced the 15-year timeline of the U.S. deal and the repayment of the debt under the Michigan agreement is estimated to take 50 years.

"There is no splitting of tolls under that [Michigan] agreement which I was referring to, perhaps imperfectly," the prime minister said.

Carney added that the cost of the new deal is "less than five per cent in present value of the overall cost of developing the bridge."

With a $6.4-billion price tag, that means the cost would be a maximum of $320 million over 15 years, or about $21 million per year, the Prime Minister's Office confirmed to CBC News.

WATCH | What we know about the deal: Gordie Howe bridge agreement released: Here’s what to know | Duration 3:18 The proposed agreement surrounding the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor, Ont., to Detroit, was released amid escalated tariff threats by U.S. President Donald Trump.

Carney's original description raised questions from the Opposition Conservatives who called for the deal to be released publicly.

Conservative MP Kelly McCauley, chair of the government operations committee, said in a social media post on Thursday that he's convening a meeting next week to launch an "urgent investigation into the details of the Gordie Howe bridge deal and the misinformation provided to Canadians about it."

Speaking to reporters shortly after Carney's news conference, Conservative House leader Andrew Scheer said the prime minister should be "embarrassed" by the deal with the U.S.

"He tried to hide this from Canadians. This is just another example of how Mark Carney is just delivering illusions for Canadians, no real results," Scheer said.

U.S. pushed back opening

U.S. President Donald Trump erupted on social media in February, posting a series of falsehoods about the bridge and saying he wouldn't allow it to open "until the United States is fully compensated for everything we have given them."

The bridge's June opening was abruptly delayed until Ottawa and Washington reached the new agreement. Trump called it "a much better deal."

Scheer called it a "major concession" and said the Liberals need to explain what Canada got out of the agreement.

But Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the deal was "critical" to open the bridge and ensure trade flows across the border.

WATCH | Conservatives slam new bridge deal: Gordie Howe bridge 'a very bad deal' for Canada: Conservative critic | Duration 2:17 Conservative Canada-U.S. relations critic Shuvaloy Majumdar said on Wednesday that sharing the revenue of the Gordie Howe International Bridge with the U.S. is one in 'a long list of bad deals' for Canada. 'It's time Canadians got a good deal,' he said.

"The prime minister did an excellent job getting this deal done, getting $300 billion of goods across the border," Ford said at the news conference with Carney.

"It's critical for all manufacturers that this bridge gets opened. He did an incredible job and I thank you for that."

Under the 15-year agreement, the U.S. portion of the revenues will go toward an economic fund, which Carney said is meant to be used to drive traffic toward the bridge.

The bridge is set to open on Monday.

World.title: 3 Canadian Armed Forces members injured after falling into crevasse at Jasper National Park
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian Armed Forces says three of its members were injured last week after falling into a crevasse during a training exercise in Jasper National Park.

Maj. Bradley Roy said the three-person rope team was performing a rescue exercise when they dropped about 20 metres into the crevasse on the Athabasca Glacier.

Roy said the three were responsive and stable and were flown to hospital.

He said it was a high-risk exercise and that rescue personnel were already at the scene in case of an accident.

Roy said an investigation is underway to determine what led to the fall and to make sure training procedures are safe and performed as planned.

Citing privacy considerations, he did not provide details on the injuries.

World.title: U.S. launches new tariff, replacing what Supreme Court struck down
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Trump administration is imposing a new global tariff regime designed to take the place of a temporary 10 per cent tariff that expires Friday.

The replacement tariffs will apply to goods from Canada, the European Union and nearly 60 other countries.

However, Canadian exports that comply with the rules of origin in the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement will be exempt. That means no change to either the rate or the scope of U.S. President Donald Trump's existing tariffs on Canadian products.

The U.S. justification for the new tariff is that the countries have failed to do enough to keep products made by forced labour out of their supply chains.

This follows a U.S. trade representative investigation this spring into whether 59 countries plus the European Union are effectively banning the importation of goods produced with forced labour.

The investigation declared that every U.S. trading partner failed to meet the bar.

'We're not in favour of sweatshops'

"We're not in favour of sweatshops, and we don't want anyone else to be in favour of it either," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNN late Thursday afternoon, shortly after announcing the tariffs.

Forced labour is just the latest of the Trump administration's shifting justifications for its tariff regimes. The changes have been forced upon them largely by the legal system, because of limits to the president's powers to impose tariffs.

The new tariffs take the place of a temporary 10 per cent levy that Trump imposed in February, immediately after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down his original global tariff regime.

That replacement tariff was time-limited to five months, so its July 24 expiration date was long-expected.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, right, tours a solar panel factory in Walbridge, Ohio, in April. Greer announced the Trump administration's latest global tariff regime on Thursday. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

The Trump administration has been searching for new, legal ways to impose broad-based tariffs since that Supreme Court loss nixed what was its "Plan A" for global tariffs.

Plan A included the so-called Liberation Day tariffs placed on dozens of countries in early 2025, as well as duties of 35 per cent on Canadian products, based on Trump's declaration that fentanyl trafficking across the northern border constituted a national emergency. The court ruled the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not give Trump the authority to levy those tariffs

Plan B was a tariff of 10 per cent, imposed under Section 122 of the U.S. Trade Act, which says the president can impose a temporary tariff to address what it describes “large and serious United States balance-of-payments deficits." That tariff is limited to a duration of 150 days without congressional approval.

Plan C involves the new forced labour tariffs, imposed under Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act, which gives the president the power to impose tariffs as relief against unfair trade practices of other countries.

The tariff rate is 10 per cent for goods from Canada and 15 other U.S. trading partners, including the European Union, the U.K., Argentina, El Salvador, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

Another 44 countries — including Japan, Singapore, India, South Korea and Vietnam — face a tariff of 12.5 per cent.

Canada has "one of the world's most robust frameworks to prevent and address forced labour," said Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc on Thursday.

"Canada shares the United States' objective of ensuring goods produced with forced labour do not enter our supply chains," LeBlanc said in a statement. "We will continue engaging constructively with the United States on this matter, as well as other outstanding issues, over the coming weeks."

The Carney government has earlier this month formally disputed the U.S. claim that Canada is allowing the import of goods made by forced labour.

'Pretext for a tariff policy'

The Trump administration's justification for the new tariff regime is "too convenient to be taken seriously," said Congressman Richard Neal of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the U.S. House Ways and Means Committee.

"Forced labour is a real and pervasive problem in our supply chains and demands serious enforcement," Neal said in a news release. "It should never be cheapened into a pretext for a tariff policy built on dubious legal theories and personal grievances."

The latest broad-based tariffs use a different section of U.S. law from the ones that give the president the power to impose tariffs on specific industrial sectors — such as steel, aluminum and autos — on the basis of U.S. national security.

They also differ from the 50 per cent tariffs that Trump is threatening to impose on billions of dollars worth of Canadian goods, under a never-before-used section of the U.S. Tariff Act of 1930.

Those tariffs, slated to take effect on Aug. 19, are based on the administration's claims that Canada is discriminating against U.S. commerce in the alcohol, dairy and auto sectors.

World.title: Body of 2nd brother who drowned in Manitoba lake has been recovered: RCMP
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After several days of searching Nutimik Lake, the body of Aaron Au Ramirez, 13, has been recovered, Manitoba RCMP say.

The boy had jumped into the water near Sturgeon Falls on Saturday after his brother Maximo, 10, slipped on some rocks and fell into the lake.

In a news release issued Thursday evening, Lac du Bonnet RCMP confirmed Aaron's body was found in the water at 7:45 p.m.

Maximo's body was found Wednesday evening.

RCMP said the family has been notified and thanked the many volunteers and supporting agencies that helped locate the two boys.

Allison Baker-Thiessen, the owner of Nutimik Lodge, where the boys' family has been staying, described the search as "a fight."

She said a community member found Aaron's body at the same time of day and in the same place where they found Maximo the day before.

A boat returns to the shore of Nutimik Lake during search efforts Thursday for Aaron Au Ramirez. The body of the 13-year-old was eventually found, at the same time and place where his younger brother's body was recovered on Wednesday. (CBC)

"We got the community together, we got all the emergency teams together. We had countless hours of people helping out and doing wellness checks and all the support in so many different angles," she said.

"Without all these people standing beside us … we couldn't do anything."

Baker-Thiessen said while Aaron's family is glad to have found his body, they are in a lot of pain.

"This is going to be a very challenging time for them," she said.

World.title: Properties destroyed by wildfire near Clinton, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A wildfire burning northwest of Clinton, B.C., has damaged or destroyed buildings on about 20 properties, says a local official.

Kevin Skrepnek, director of emergency operations for the Thompson-Nicola Regional District (TNRD), said the damage happened last Friday and it ranges from melted siding on a structure to all buildings on a property being burned down.

“The number of structures [destroyed] is likely, you know, dozens. And in some cases, unfortunately those were houses,” he said.

Officials surveyed the properties soon after the Fiftynine Creek fire ripped through the area, he said, and then contacted the owners. News of the destruction was then shared more widely at a community meeting Thursday.

“This fire is still quite active. So it's not to say that we won't have more damage in the days and weeks ahead,” Skrepnek added.

The Fiftynine Creek fire, pictured on July 21. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

The fire that spans more than 108 square kilometres has forced the evacuation of the area around Big Bar Lake, while the entire village of Clinton, with a population of several hundred, was placed on evacuation alert late Wednesday.

The B.C. Wildfire Service said crews fighting the Big Bar Complex fires, which include the French Bar Creek and Pear Lake wildfires, were being challenged by hot and dry conditions, and further growth and an increase in fire activity were expected on Thursday.

Mikhail Elsay, an information officer with the service, said crews were focused on trying to hold the Fiftynine Creek fire to just south of Big Bar Road.

"Our crew is currently engaged in a bit of a firefight there to try to keep the fire from travelling any further north," he told the briefing.

The fire had burned up to control lines on the fire's northern flank, Elsay added.

The wildfire service said conditions were particularly challenging near the fire's southeast corner.

Crews were continuing to protect properties northwest of Big Bar Lake and along the Big Bar Road corridor, and helicopters were helping slow the spread of the fire.

Family steps up to feed wildfire crews

As crews work to contain the fire, Nick Kosovic and his mother Maria, who operate the Stagecoach Cafe in Clinton, have been battling since Saturday to keep the firefighters' bellies full.

“We have been working about 18 hours a day feeding wildfire fighters as they’ve been coming, gradually growing in number, and finally they've got their camp cook all set up so we are somewhat off the hook," Nick told Carolina de Ryk on CBC's Radio West.

Nick said he and his mother have been sleeping in shifts as they try to fuel fire crews for their intense days in the field.

“These men and women, they eat like horses, they are burning maybe 3,000, 4,000, 5,000 calories a day, so they’re not just normal meals," he said.

“We’re talking a quarter of a lasagna each.”

Despite the long days, Maria said the work has been rewarding — and the whole community has stepped up to help.

“It has been an amazing situation where friends are calling me, 'Do you need anything? I’m shopping in Kamloops, I’m shopping in Ashcroft,' and they bring the groceries to us," she said.

“They are doing this for the … firefighters we have here, the men and women working so hard for us. We highly appreciate it.”

While Nick was initially sleeping at the café because of the long days, he's now there out of necessity after his home was placed under an evacuation order due to the fire.

Around 65 firefighters, 13 helicopters, 57 heavy equipment vehicles and 77 structure protection resources were fighting the fires as of Thursday.

World.title: What’s become of the Toronto Blue Jays? With 2 months left, some fans are giving up hope
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Less than a year after nearly becoming champions of baseball, and with 60 games left to play, the season-long assessment of what's gone wrong with the 2026 Toronto Blue Jays is already beginning to feel like a post-mortem.

Coming out of the All-Star break with the worst record in its division, the team needed to push to get back in the playoff race. But the Jays have gone 1-5 since then and are at risk of being swept at home Thursday afternoon, a possible nail in the coffin.

The situation this week prompted the Blue Jays Today podcast to ask on social media platform X: "Blue Jays Fans... Is the season over?"

A fair question. With over two months still left to play, the Toronto Blue Jays now have no chance to repeat as division champs, and only 7.2 per cent odds of making the post-season at all, according to sports statistics site FanGraphs, an online resource for baseball statistics.

Through the first 102 games, the defending American League champions haven't been doing a whole lot of defending. And fans who expected another deep run this October are turning from disgruntled to resigned.

“Does anyone kinda wish the selling would just start so we can get the pain over with, like ripping off a Band-Aid?” one Redditor asked Wednesday, ahead of the Aug. 3 Major League Baseball trade deadline, where the Jays were until recently expected to be buyers preparing for October.

So what happened? And how are Blue Jays fans processing it all?

Dome still filling up for losing team. But at what cost?

Hopes were beyond high coming into 2026.

The Jays had come within two outs — and mere inches — of winning the World Series last fall. The organization then lost star shortstop Bo Bichette, but bolstered the roster with high-profile, off-season signings that signalled a willingness to take another shot at the title.

"We're riding in after the World Series expecting another one, and expecting that this will be the World Series we win," superfan Lesley Mak told CBC News in March, a far cry from the sentiment among most Jays fans in July.

(@JGoldberg12/X)

Season ticket and quarter-season ticket packages were nearly sold out before opening day, and demand for single-game tickets was high.

That's kept seats filled, and expensive, even as the team has stumbled more and more through the summer.

Injuries and an unexpected slide in hitting and fielding have made the team frustrating to watch. But even as the losses pile up, diehard fans haven't had the consolation of picking up cheap seats and enjoying a lazy, last-minute outing at the park.

(@JRoc23/X)

Large Rogers Centre crowds keep showing up. They've watched star player after star player fall to injury. They've watched the lowest-scoring club in baseball get shut out and routed again and again.

One thing hometown fans haven't seen: Vladdy hit the ball out of the park.

Slumping slugger(s)

For a man whose hard hits and joyful passion for the game has solidified him as the loveable, heart and soul of the franchise, the decline has been quick, shocking and hard to watch.

After one of the hottest Octobers any hitter has had in recent memory, Vladimir Guerrero Jr., has so far hit only six home runs — none of them at home.

The $500-million star slugger has, simply put, been neither a star nor slugger, taking increasing heat from fans upset on a poor return for his high salary.

(@KPapetti/X)

The lack of production has occasionally resulted in something that was unthinkable last October: Toronto fans booing Vladdy.

Guerrero Jr. has said he's been playing through lower back issues. He declined his invitation to this year's All-Star Game, saying he needed to recuperate. (The baseball world had been up in arms about his selection in the first place, with accusations Canadian fans were stuffing the ballot box to get the low-performing first baseman on the roster).

Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has a disappointing slugging percentage of .347 and on-base-plus-slugging percentage of .645 as of Thursday. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)

It's not just Vladdy. Plenty of other Blue Jays have failed to live up to their tremendous 2025 performances, including Dalton Varsho, George Springer and Alejandro Kirk. And long-term injuries to other sluggers like Anthony Santander and Addison Barger have also put more pressure on others to pick up the slack.

But the Jays will need Vladdy to come to life if they have any chance of bouncing back.

There have been far more remarkable comebacks, with the club a surmountable 6 1/2 games out of the final American League wildcard spot as of Thursday. The roster is still close to the one that made a run last year, and a few players like Dylan Cease, Louis Varland and Ernie Clement have been great.

But they will need to overcome surprisingly poor fielding and hitting to recapture a bit of that 2025 magic and pull themselves back into it. Call it optimistic, call it delusional, but even after a fourth straight loss Wednesday, not all fans have given up.

World.title: Jewish advocacy organization, North Bay mayor condemn 'Bigotfest' planned near the city
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. The mayor of North Bay and a Jewish advocacy organization are condemning a weekend gathering that appears to be taking place somewhere in the area— that organizers themselves are calling “Bigotfest”— saying hate and discrimination have no place in the community. The three-day event, scheduled for July 24 to 26, has been promoted on social media by prominent members and associates of Second Sons Canada, a group that describes itself as a “Canadian men’s nationalist club” founded in 2024. On its website, Second Sons says it’s committed to defending what it claims is a threatened way of life through political activism and fitness training. “We're deeply concerned with the rise of the Second Sons and with the danger that they present to Canadian society," said Richard Robertson, B'nai Brith Canada’s director of research and advocacy. "They’re opposed to Canadian values, they’re virulently racist, they’re anti-Semitic." He said the Jewish advocacy organization learned of “Bigotfest” through its ongoing monitoring of extremist activity and believes this event is an attempt to normalize hateful ideology. An event called "Bigotfest" has been promoted on social media by prominent members and associates of Second Sons Canda. This image was posted to X by Morgan Guptill, partner of Diagolon founder and Second Sons president Jeremy MacKenzie. (Morgan Guptill/X) Second Sons was inspired by militant white nationalist groups in other countries, according to the Canadian Anti-Hate Network. A previous CBC visual investigation found leaders of the organization welcome neo-Nazis into the group, call the official statistics of the Holocaust the product of “propagandists,” use racist slurs and say Canadian politicians should be executed. The Institute for Strategic Dialogue, an international think tank that studies extremism, describes Second Sons’ ideology as rooted in conspiratorial claims that white populations are being replaced by non-white people “through a combination of immigration, procreation and policy decisions.” “Discrimination has no place in North Bay,” says mayor Promotional material posted on various social media platforms advertises “Bigotfest” as “family fun for all,” with attendees invited to camp in tents or trailers while taking part in activities including fights, a pig roast, pugil stick competitions, knife throwing and children’s games. While the exact location has not been confirmed, associates and members of Second Sons have said the event is set to take place somewhere in North Bay. North Bay Mayor Peter Chirico said the city is aware of information circulating online about a possible event, but has not confirmed whether it is actually taking place or where it may be held. Public Safety Statement: Safe & Lawful Gatherings
🔗https://t.co/0QN22pRTJk pic.twitter.com/r2P6l7eUol —NorthBayPolice “I want to be clear that, if this event is taking place, it is not taking place on municipal property,” Chirico said in a statement to CBC News. “Any activity intended to promote racism, hate or discrimination has no place in North Bay. Our community values respect, inclusion and the right of everyone to feel safe and welcome.” Chirico said the city has been in contact with North Bay Police, which is aware of the information circulating online. In a media release, North Bay Police said they are aware of a possible gathering involving individuals “whose views have raised community concerns.” “The right to lawful expression and peaceful assembly is protected under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms,” the statement reads. “Police remain impartial and are committed to protecting these rights while ensuring the safety and security of everyone in our community.” The police service said there’s an important distinction between expression that may be offensive or unpopular and behaviour that constitutes a criminal offence. “Threats, violence, hate-motivated offences, or any other criminal behaviour will not be tolerated,” said North Bay Police. “Any suspected criminal activity will be thoroughly investigated and may result in arrests and charges.” Police are encouraging people to avoid confronting individuals associated with the gathering and instead report suspicious or criminal behaviour. Second Sons Canada members pose in front of a downtown Sudbury parking garage. The group published the photo with the faces of most members blurred. (Second Sons Canada/Telegram) The latest planned gathering comes just weeks after Second Sons drew criticism for appearing at a Sudbury memorial dedicated to people who have died from drug overdoses. Images shared online by the group showed members posing outside a downtown parking garage covered in graffiti featuring the word “remigration” and stencilled images of Adolf Hitler. 'Awful but lawful' "Bigotfest" is also expected to feature a "trade show" with vendors from "local businesses." Social media posts mention an online business that sells magnets and stickers bearing slogans including “mass deportations now,” “I wish I was speaking German” and “racism could save your life" is planning to attend. The event poster also promises vendors selling Diagolon merchandise. That group was named in a 2022 House of Commons report as an example of "ideologically motivated violent extremism." “This is organizers trying to bring together those who have hateful and racist views to advance their ideology and really to monetize hate, selling merchandise with hateful slogans on it,” Robertson said. “That has no place in our society.” He added that events like this can embolden extremists by providing opportunities to network, recruit supporters and normalize racist and antisemitic beliefs in public settings. "Just because something might be awful, but lawful, doesn't mean that it's any less dangerous or that it should be ignored," Robertson said. CBC News contacted the organizers seeking comment and asking about the event’s purpose and their reaction to the characterizations made by B’nai Brith Canada. A response sent from an email address associated with the organizers of “Bigotfest” did not answer those questions.

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement

Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.
