World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: World Bank estimates $19.6 billion in earthquake damage in Venezuela
World.content:
World Bank estimates $19.6 billion in earthquake damage in Venezuela

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 22:37 UTC Full article

The disaster struck a country with a poverty rate above 76% and an economy that contracted sharply over the past decade, in a period marked by US sanctions

The twin earthquakes that struck northern Venezuela on June 24 caused an estimated $19.6 billion in direct physical damage, according to a preliminary assessment published on Thursday by the World Bank. The figure is equivalent to about 18% of the country's gross domestic product, based on International Monetary Fund data.

The report, produced using the institution's rapid damage estimation methodology, attributes 47% of the losses to residential buildings, 27% to infrastructure, and 26% to non-residential buildings. La Guaira state and the Capital District, which includes Caracas, account for roughly half of the total impact. In La Guaira, the hardest-hit area, the institution estimates that one in five homes was destroyed.

The estimate does not include the costs of rebuilding with structural improvements or of debris removal, which the World Bank says could amount to between two and two and a half times the replacement value, bringing the total bill to close to $50 billion. An early United Nations assessment, released a week after the quakes, had put direct damage at $37 billion.

“This assessment provides the Government of Venezuela and its partners with an early, objective basis for recovery planning,” said Susana Cordeiro Guerra, the institution's vice-president for Latin America and the Caribbean, adding that the earthquakes “have disrupted lives, damaged critical infrastructure, and created new challenges” for the country.

The earthquakes, of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5, left 5,398 dead and 16,740 injured according to official figures, which authorities present as provisional, while unofficial estimates put the number of missing in the thousands. About 18,000 people remain without housing. It is the deadliest quake recorded in Venezuela since 1812. The United Nations estimates that more than a million people need immediate humanitarian assistance.

The disaster struck a country with a poverty rate above 76% and an economy that contracted sharply over the past decade, in a period marked by US sanctions. The World Bank warned that, at current levels of public and private investment, reconstruction would stretch beyond ten years, with lasting effects on economic activity, and called for a rapid increase in public funding.

The report was published after fourteen US Democratic lawmakers asked President Donald Trump to lift economic sanctions on Venezuela and facilitate the country's access to its frozen assets abroad. A hundred economists signed a request along the same lines. The institution said it is working with the Venezuelan government, the Inter-American Development Bank, and CAF to define additional technical and financial support.

World.title: US rebuilds its tariff wall with forced-labor levies on 60 economies
World.content:
US rebuilds its tariff wall with forced-labor levies on 60 economies

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 22:33 UTC Full article

The levies are applied under Section 301 of the 1974 trade law, which allows a response to unfair trade practices following an investigation

The United States imposed tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on 60 trading partners, which together account for about 99% of its imports, over what the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) described as their failure to adopt and effectively enforce bans on the import of goods produced with forced labor. The measures, announced on Thursday, took effect at 12:01 a.m. on Friday, at the same moment the 10% universal tariff in place since February expired.

The levies are applied under Section 301 of the 1974 trade law, which allows a response to unfair trade practices following an investigation. The move is the biggest effort by Donald Trump's administration to rebuild its tariff framework after the Supreme Court struck down his “reciprocal” tariffs in February, finding that the administration had exceeded its authority by invoking an emergency powers law. The temporary tariff that replaced them, issued under Section 122, was valid for 150 days without congressional approval.

The final breakdown sets a 10% tariff for seventeen economies that adopted restrictions or committed to doing so — among them Canada, Mexico, the United Kingdom, and India — effective rates of 10% to 12.5% depending on the product for another five, and 12.5% for the remaining 38. Several countries changed their legislation after the proposal was made public in June and moved to the lower band; India, for instance, had initially been placed at 12.5%. Oil and gas, fertilizers, and goods qualifying as duty-free under the North American trade agreement are exempt, as are goods in transit.

“The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it's well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” said Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who argued the action corrects “both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice.” A senior official, speaking on condition of anonymity, described it as the most significant international labor-rights action undertaken by any country.

Several partners rejected the accusation. The European Union dismissed it explicitly even before the final determination. Tariffs are paid by US companies importing the products, which typically pass the cost on to consumer prices.

The measure adds to other recent actions under the same legal instrument: the 25% tariffs on most Brazilian products took effect on Wednesday, and this week Trump signed proclamations to apply additional 50% levies in 30 days on a range of Canadian goods. Several companies are expected to challenge the new round in court.

World.title: New York judge sets June 2027 for the start of Maduro and Cilia Flores's trial
World.content:
New York judge sets June 2027 for the start of Maduro and Cilia Flores's trial

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 07:34 UTC Full article

Maduro, 63, is charged with conspiracy to commit narcoterrorism, cocaine importation, and possession of machine guns and destructive devices

Federal Judge Alvin Hellerstein set June 1, 2027, as the preliminary start date for the trial of former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in the narcoterrorism case they face in the United States. The decision came on Wednesday during the case's third hearing before the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, which lasted only a few minutes.

Maduro, 63, is charged with conspiracy to commit narcoterrorism, cocaine importation, and possession of machine guns and destructive devices. Flores, 69, faces charges linked to drug importation and weapons possession. Both have pleaded not guilty to all counts and have been held at a federal prison in Brooklyn since January 3, when they were captured in Caracas during a US military operation.

The schedule, jointly proposed by prosecutors and the defense the previous day, contemplates two rounds of pretrial motions. The defense will file a first set before September 2 arguing Maduro's immunity as the head of a sovereign state, one of its central contentions. According to his lawyer, Barry Pollack, if that motion succeeds, the second round would not be necessary. Prosecutors expect to complete the handover of unclassified evidence by September 22 and of classified material by November 15. Hellerstein called a hearing for November 17 to debate those arguments.

“This is a realistic schedule, we don't think it will be delayed,” Pollack said, after the judge voiced doubts about the parties' ability to meet the deadlines set for submitting evidence, witnesses, and experts.

Demonstrators for and against the proceedings gathered near the courthouse, with police present to prevent incidents, as had happened at the March hearing. From Caracas, the former president's son and lawmaker for the governing PSUV, Nicolás Maduro Guerra, called the process “unjust” and demanded his parents' release.

The case earlier saw a dispute over funding for the defense: Maduro and Flores argued they could not pay private lawyers because of US sanctions and because they were barred from using Venezuelan state funds. In April, Washington authorized Venezuela to cover their legal representation.

Since the capture, Venezuela has been governed by former vice-president Delcy Rodríguez, under whose tenure the United States eased sanctions on the oil industry. The former president also faces other civil proceedings in the United States: last week, a Miami judge issued a default judgment ordering him, along with other officials, to pay $314 million to three US citizens.

World.title: Wes Streeting appointed UK Defence Secretary; ‘disappointment’ with removal of Dan Jarvis, responsible for DIP
World.content:
Wes Streeting appointed UK Defence Secretary; ‘disappointment’ with removal of Dan Jarvis, responsible for DIP

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 07:34 UTC Full article

“With John Healey now looking after the money, Wes Streeting can focus on the vital Defence Reforms necessary to deliver.”

Former Health and Social Care Secretary Wes Streeting has been appointed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham as the new UK Defense Secretary, replacing Dan Jarvis who has taken the job when John Healey resigned last June.

This means Jarvis was Defence Secretary for less than six weeks – but in that time he was responsible for publishing the long awaited Defense Investment Plan (DIP), and there was expectation across the forces whether PM Burnham would keep his in Defense..

However taking to social media after it was announced that Streeting would replace him in the role, Mr Jarvis said: “It’s been an immense honor to serve as Defense Secretary and again be amongst those who give everything to defend our nation.”

“We owe them a huge debt of gratitude — and they will always have my absolute support. I wish my successor every success in this vital role.”

Former conservative Defence Secretary Ben Wallace criticized Mr Burnham’s decision to replace Mr Jarvis .

“Removing Dan Jarvis to find a spot for Wes Streeting shows a contempt for Defense at a time they need continuity and someone who understands the new way of warfare and the men and women of the armed forces,” he posted on X.

But there was a more positive reaction to the news from retired Air Marshal Greg Bagwell, a former combat pilot and senior leader in the RAF, who said: “With John Healey now looking after the money, Wes Streeting can focus on the vital Defense Reforms necessary to deliver.”

Meanwhile, a former head of the British Army has also said he is “disappointed” that Wes Streeting has been made defense secretary but spoke more positively about the potential relationship between Mr Streeting and his predecessor in the Treasury.

Lord Dannatt told Times Radio: “A new defense secretary has a lot to learn – the defense portfolio is one of the more complicated ones in government and as far as I’m aware Wes Streeting has got no background in defense, no background in the military”. (Forces)

World.title: Stephen Doughty confirmed as Minister of State for Overseas Territories
World.content:
Stephen Doughty confirmed as Minister of State for Overseas Territories

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 02:00 UTC Full article

Minister Doughty during a meeting in London with MLA Roger Spink

Stephen Doughty MP has been confirmed at Minister of State in the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office. Until 21 July 2026 and from 8 July 2024 he was previously Minister of State for Europe, North America and Overseas Territories in the FCDO.

Stephen was first elected as Welsh Labour and Co-operative Member of Parliament for Cardiff South and Penarth in November 2012.

Stephen studied at Lester B. Pearson UWC in Canada, Oxford University and St Andrews University. He later worked for the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly and for members of the then National Assembly for Wales.

Stephen spent a number of years working for humanitarian and international development NGOs World Vision UK, Oxfam GB, Oxfam International and Oxfam Cymru. During the previous Labour government he was Special Adviser to the Secretary of State for International Development.

Stephen served at the Wales, Home Affairs, Arms Export Controls and International Development Committees in Parliament. He was also an opposition Whip and a Shadow Minister for Trade and Industry. He chaired the All-Party Parliamentary Group for HIV and Aids, and was a member of the British-Irish Parliamentary Assembly.

Stephen completed the Armed Forces Parliamentary scheme, attending the Royal College of Defense Studies 2017 to 2018. He has also served as an Army Reservist. In 2020 he was appointed Shadow Foreign Affairs and International Development Minister and in 2021 he was appointed Shadow Minister for Europe, North America and the Overseas Territories.

Stephen Doughty as Minister for Europe last week signed the UK/EU treaty on Gibraltar, ensuring ministerial continuity at the FCDO. Gibraltar media reported his reappointment is significant in the implementation phase of the treaty and when the treaty comes to be ratified by the House of Commons under the process set out in the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010.

As a UK Government minister, Mr Doughty was closely involved in the final phases of the negotiation on the treaty and has close knowledge of the matter. He is also well versed in Gibraltar issues, having visited the Rock on numerous occasions in recent years including for National Day celebrations.

“I’m delighted to see that Stephen has been reappointed to the post of Minister for Europe,” said Chief Minister Fabian Picardo, reacting to the news. “He has a deep knowledge of the issues affecting Gibraltar from his time in Opposition and in Government.”

World.title: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, no friend of “Trumpism”, White House
World.content:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, no friend of “Trumpism”, White House

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 01:57 UTC Full article

Miliband’s political positions have frequently put him at odds with the White House: he led opposition within the National Security Council to the use of UK bases for US bombers

Reports from the United States indicate the White House has raised concerns about UK Premier Andy Burnham’s decision to appoint Ed Miliband as foreign secretary, amid warnings from the Donald Trump administration that he could create tensions in the UK-US relationship, according to reports Tuesday.

One senior US official reportedly told the Telegraph that Miliband would be a “point of friction” because of his support for green energy policies that Trump has criticized.

The warning is understood to have been made during unofficial “access” talks between the Trump administration and Burnham’s team after it became clear that Burnham was the leading candidate to replace Keir Starmer.

Miliband’s political positions have frequently put him at odds with the White House. In February, he led opposition within the National Security Council to the use of UK bases for US bombers, a dispute that contributed to a deterioration in Starmer’s relationship with the president, who described the prime minister as “not Winston Churchill.”

The opposition resulted in Starmer denying a US request to use Diego Garcia, the strategically significant military base in the Chagos Islands, at the beginning of the US’ and Israel’s war on Iran.

Miliband has also faced criticism from Trump allies for his approach to energy policy. As energy secretary, he blocked new licenses for oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, a move at odds with Trump’s support for increased domestic fossil fuel production.

The foreign secretary’s previous comments about Trump have also come under scrutiny. In 2016, Miliband wrote, “We must do our best at home and abroad to resist the worst of Trumpism … These are dark days for America and the world. There can be little solace right now.”

In 2017, Miliband said Trump had “lowered the bar for idiocy” and later joined a Stop Trump March in London.

World.title: Report says Trump is pushing Infantino to lead the UN
World.content:
Report says Trump is pushing Infantino to lead the UN

22nd Wednesday, July 2026 - 22:26 UTC Full article

According to those sources, Trump believes the football official, 56, who holds dual Swiss and Italian nationality, is “respected by everyone around the world”

US President Donald Trump is promoting FIFA President Gianni Infantino as a candidate to succeed António Guterres at the head of the United Nations, according to the New York Post, which cited anonymous sources close to the White House. The information has not been officially confirmed by the US government or FIFA, and Infantino himself has not commented publicly.

According to those sources, Trump believes the football official, 56, who holds dual Swiss and Italian nationality, is “respected by everyone around the world” and has “a special ability to bring people together.” The president's special envoy for global partnerships, Paolo Zampolli, endorsed the idea in remarks to the same newspaper, the only openly stated backing so far.

Any such candidacy would face procedural and political hurdles. The next secretary-general must first secure a recommendation from the Security Council, where the United States holds veto power, before being confirmed by the General Assembly. Guterres leaves office on December 31, at the end of his second term.

The proposal would also upend an established expectation in multilateral diplomacy. Under the informal regional rotation norm governing the appointment, the next secretary-general had been expected to come from Latin America and the Caribbean. Names in circulation include former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet, Mexico's Alicia Bárcena, Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, Ecuador's María Fernanda Espinosa, and Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, as well as Argentina's Rafael Grossi, director of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Infantino, who has led FIFA since 2016, has already announced his intention to seek a third term at the organization. His relationship with Trump grew closer during the 2026 World Cup, hosted by the United States, Mexico, and Canada. FIFA opened an office in Trump Tower in New York, and Infantino presented the president with the first Peace Prize created by the body, last December. The two appeared together at Sunday's final award ceremony, when they handed the trophy to Spain.

That proximity drew controversy during the tournament. Trump called Infantino to request a review of the red card given to US forward Folarin Balogun, after which FIFA's disciplinary committee suspended the ban, an unprecedented decision that drew criticism from UEFA and other federations.

Across his two terms, Trump has maintained a tense relationship with the United Nations and has questioned the role of multilateral bodies, in addition to withdrawing the United States from the Paris Agreement and the World Health Organization.

World.title: A young Falkland Islander will represent the islands at the Commonwealth Youth Parliament in Sydney
World.content:
A young Falkland Islander will represent the islands at the Commonwealth Youth Parliament in Sydney

22nd Wednesday, July 2026 - 22:13 UTC Full article

Lee is a Falkland Islands student currently studying veterinary nursing in the United Kingdom and serves as a junior ambassador for the islands (Pic FB)

The Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly announced that Jessica Lee will represent the territory at the Commonwealth Youth Parliament, to be held from July 26 to 31 in Sydney, hosted by the Parliament of New South Wales, Australia.

Lee is a Falkland Islands student currently studying veterinary nursing in the United Kingdom and serves as a junior ambassador for the islands. According to the official statement, she brings to the role first-hand experience of life in Camp — as the rural area outside Stanley is known locally — as well as of farming, tourism, and conservation work. She has previously represented the islands in engagements with the Speaker of the British House of Commons and took part in an exchange of correspondence with schools in Argentina. In 2025 she was named Apprentice of the Year.

During the week of activities, the delegate will join representatives from across the Commonwealth in a full programme within the New South Wales Parliament, including caucus sessions, committee debate, and a whole-house sitting on a bill concerning artificial intelligence and democratic integrity. The agenda also includes cultural and diplomatic engagements, among them a reception at the British Consulate-General in Sydney.

“Jessica representing the Falklands in Sydney is the kind of opportunity we are proud that young Falkland Islanders have,” said Member of the Legislative Assembly Stacy Bragger, portfolio holder for Education and Community. He added that this kind of international representation sends, in his view, “a strong message” overseas about what he described as the everyday reality of self-determination in the islands' community.

The delegate herself expressed enthusiasm for the experience. “I am really looking forward to meeting my other Youth Parliament members and getting to represent my home on the global stage,” she said, adding that she is interested in politics and hopes to learn about other countries' cultures and stories.

The Commonwealth Youth Parliament is an annual activity that brings together young delegates from the organization's countries and territories to simulate the workings of a parliament, with debates on bills and legislative procedure.

The Falklands, a British overseas territory in the South Atlantic, take part in various Commonwealth activities. The archipelago is the subject of a sovereignty dispute between the United Kingdom and Argentina, which claims the islands and maintains that the question should be settled through bilateral negotiations. This is the second public statement the Assembly has issued this week, following its congratulations to the new British prime minister, Andy Burnham.

World.title: Mexico intercepts a trafficking scheme smuggling native ants to SE Asia
World.content:
Mexican authorities have intercepted Amazon parrots, peacock turtles, howler monkeys and even baby crocodiles in recent years, but the country’s latest case of illegal wildlife trafficking centers on a far smaller animal: queen ants.

Earlier this month, environmental officials in the west-central state of Jalisco seized 105 queen ants hidden inside plastic toys and labeled as “collectible figures” in a shipment bound for Southeast Asia, the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa) said.

The discovery was made July 9 after a parcel company flagged a suspicious package in El Salto, Jalisco, outside Guadalajara. The package was addressed to Laos, a landlocked country between Vietnam and Thailand.

Inside, inspectors found the insects sealed in individual test tubes and concealed within toy figures, including one containing 22 tubes and another with 83. Each small tube appeared to contain cotton and moisture, the standard way to house queen ants in test tubes.

Experts determined that it was not feasible to keep so many ants alive in that manner because of their biological needs.

According to a Profepa press release, 87 ants survived and were later released into the Cerro Viejo Protected Natural Area, while 18 died.

The seized ants belong to the genus Pogonomyrmex and are commonly known as harvester ants. They are native to Mexico and play a role in seed dispersal and soil health in arid ecosystems.

The seized ants fit into a growing niche hobby in Europe and Asia, where buyers use queen ants to stock formicariums, specialized terrariums that house and display ant colonies. Owners watch the ants build tunnels, haul seeds and care for larvae.

The ant farms are promoted as do-it-yourself ecosystems built around a single fertilized queen, which can eventually produce thousands of workers.

Collectors and hobbyists sometimes pay 200 to 400 pesos (US $11 to $22) for a queen ant online, while more exotic ants can fetch up to 1,200 pesos (US $68), according to the newspaper El Sol de México.

Illegal wildlife trafficking remains a major issue in Mexico. Authorities have seized hundreds of turtles on highways and at airports, along with parrots, reptiles and other species trafficked through parcel services and border crossings.

The numbers especially surged during the coronavirus pandemic, according to Profepa.

Globally, illegal wildlife trafficking affects more than 4,000 plant and animal species in at least 162 countries and territories, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. Some assessments have valued the illegal wildlife trade at up to US $23 billion a year.

Despite the enforcement action in Jalisco, no arrests have been reported so far.

“Profepa will follow up on the corresponding administrative procedure,” the agency stated, adding that it will continue to fight illegal wildlife trafficking through surveillance and other means.

With reports from El Sol de México and Milenio

World.title: Oaxaca journalist, known for criticizing governor, shot dead; Feds takes over the case
World.content:
Journalist Francisco Alejandro Leyva was shot and killed Wednesday in San Pablo Etla, a suburb of Oaxaca city, the second media figure slain in Mexico in less than a week.

Leyva, a former executive producer of the Oaxacan Radio and Television Corporation, was attacked while eating breakfast at a street food stand. The gunmen escaped on a motorcycle.

The 60-year-old was well-known for his column “El zumbido de moscardón” (“The buzzing of a bumblebee”), in which he critically analyzed political life and corruption in the state of Oaxaca.

Hours after his murder, state prosecutors said video intelligence had already been uncovered from local CCTV. On Thursday, the Federal Attorney General’s Office said it would take over the investigation at the request of Oaxaca authorities, assigning it to the Specialized Prosecutor’s Office for Human Rights.

As of noon Thursday, authorities had not cited a motive for the murder nor reported any arrests.

Leyva published his final article on Tuesday night, addressing insecurity in the state and the alleged interference of organized crime in local economies and politics.

In this text, he discussed the violence in Oaxaca in the context of the Guelaguetza, calling the annual Indigenous cultural festival a failure due to government mismanagement and security issues.

Just over a year ago, Leyva filed a formal complaint with the state Human Rights Ombudsman’s Office about receiving death threats. He linked these threats to the public smear campaign he faced from regular criticism lobbed at him by Oaxaca Governor Salomón Jara during the latter’s daily press conferences.

For his part, Governor Jara condemned Wednesday’s attack, saying “[Leyva] was a journalist critical of our government (…) but no difference with the practice of journalism can ever justify an act of violence.”

International press associations also condemned the murder. Reporters without Borders said “The murder of seven journalists in just over six months is evidence of a serious and sustained failure of the Mexican state,” while calling on the federal government to present “a national emergency plan.”

📣 ARTICLE 19 condena el asesinato del periodista Alejandro Leyva Aguilar, exdirector de la Corporación Oaxaqueña de Radio y Televisión (CORTV), autor de la columna El Zumbido del Moscardón, ocurrido esta mañana, en el municipio de San Pablo Etlan, #OaxacaDeJuárez 🧵 pic.twitter.com/Z3gDePuLTY — ARTICLE 19 México y Centroamérica (@article19mxca) July 22, 2026

More than half a dozen journalists have been killed in Mexico this year, five of them since June 11. Josué Martínez, executive producer of Noticias San Martín Texmelucan, was gunned down in the state of Puebla on July 16.

Reuters news agency described Mexico as “one of the ​most dangerous countries in the world for journalists outside active war zones,” adding that “the vast majority of crimes against journalists go unpunished.”

With reports from El País, El Universal, Latinus, Aristegui Noticias and Milenio

World.title: Conservation advocates celebrate a ‘Night of the Bats’ in Oaxaca
World.content:
On June 20, as Pride parades filled the streets, the team at Proyecto LAM was preparing for their annual “Noche de los Murciélagos” (“Night of the Bats”).

Proyecto LAM is a vibrant plant nursery in Santa Catarina Minas, Oaxaca, founded in 2018 by Graciela Ángeles and her family, who produce Real Minero. Graciela explains that originally, the project focused on studying the agave plant; then “as a side effect, the need arose to study its pollinators, especially the bats.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Real Minero (@realminerooficial)

Guests are invited for a sunset walk through the garden before a series of presentations, dinner and mezcal.

The underrated importance of bats

Each year, they invite specialists to speak on the garden’s themes: its plants, pests and pollinators. This year, Irene Martínez Velasco spoke about the genetics of agave before Rosario Aceves Íñiguez, a biologist from Guadalajara, led an introduction to bats. She discussed the ecological significance and diversity of bats before emphasizing some of the challenges faced by bat populations.

Rosario says she considers bats to be one of the most misunderstood groups of mammals, “despite also being among the most fascinating, interesting and wonderful.”

Bats play a fundamental ecological role in the maintenance and functioning of ecosystems, yet they remain one of the most undervalued groups of mammals. In Mexico, where agave plays an iconic role, bats are invaluable. Nectar-feeding bats and agaves share a close ecological relationship where bats act as primary pollinators. Preserving this bond is vital for agave biodiversity and the survival of endangered bat species.

Bats’ role in agave propagation

Graciela says that “declines in bat populations threaten the survival of the agaves, particularly those propagated solely through seeds.” Agave spirits producers can support bat populations by allowing a percentage of agaves to flower and go to seed to support nectar-feeding bats. “Bat Friendly” is a certification that promotes conservation and encourages consumer participation in tequila and mezcal, while initiatives such as the one noted above encourage the producers of these liquors to adopt sustainable practices.

However, fear surrounding bats follows this unfairly maligned mammal. Myths of blood-sucking vampires and perceptions like dirty “flying rats” plague bats and those trying to help them. Ongoing stigma and their nocturnal behaviors make bats difficult to study.

Studying bats also has significant challenges. Rosario explains that “national insecurity and forced disappearances hinder field research.” She says fieldwork using capture methods has become more complicated because work is done at night, which implies greater risk. “There has been a shift towards other techniques that do not require capture, but in projects where it is possible to record or work with bats, many studies and research projects require having the specimens in hand.”

Habitat loss and other challenges for bat populations

A major concern is habitat loss. Rosario described how this reduces the number of places where bats can roost and limits food sources. Monocrops, like the agave plants used for tequila, with significant levels of pesticides, are also hurting bat populations.

Disease is also having a significant impact, in particular “white-nose syndrome,” a fungal disease that primarily affects cave-dwelling bats. According to Rosario, “over the last decade, this has led to the deaths of millions of individuals in various regions of the world.” In Oaxaca alone, it is suspected of causing a drastic decline in bat populations.

Rosario’s concerns about bat populations were echoed by Graciela. She informed the group that over the past three years, the number of bats they have found during these activities has plummeted. “During the first capture in 2018, there were several hundred bats. Last year, we only managed to capture three bats. This year, 15 were captured.”

Fortunately, there are endeavors to conserve bat populations. Conservation efforts prioritize what Graciela describes as “citizen science,” which involves making scientific data accessible to the public and facilitating knowledge sharing between farmers, producers and academics. Events like the “Noche de los Murciélagos” bring the public closer to science through workshops, talks and bat-monitoring demonstrations. These efforts help to foster awareness of the bat-agave connection.

Teaching kids (and adults) about the beauty of bats

This year, they held a contest with students from the middle school in Santa Catarina Minas to make artwork about bats. They awarded certificates and sketchbooks to the winners. For Graciela, this is a way to “influence these young people to develop their creative skills, whether through writing or drawing, and at the same time bring them into a scientific activity.” She says, “I think one of the most important things is that this year we had so many children visit. It’s something beautiful that young people are interested in science.”

Rosario says that the public can contribute by “learning about the ecological importance of bats, avoiding the destruction of their roosts, promoting their conservation and supporting initiatives and products that encourage practices friendly to these species.”

During the evening, Rosario and the team from Proyecto LAM used techniques like “mist-netting” to capture and identify species. They recorded data on the bat’s weight, sex and size, which helps document the health and presence of local populations over time. It was fascinating to watch them at work.

‘Intrepid pollinators’ released into the night

Once they had made their assessments, the bats were fed some sugar water before being released back into the wild. Rosario held each bat, and there was a brief pause before they took off into the night. It was surprisingly moving to see these fragile animals spread their wings as they realized they were free again.

Hopefully, events like “Noche de los Murciélagos” will continue to inspire people to learn about bats. Not as stigmatized creatures of the night, but as the intrepid pollinators that help maintain our diverse and beautiful ecosystem. As Graciela warns, without bats, we won’t have agave — or mezcal!

World.title: Report: Mexico-born population of US drops to 11.1 million
World.content:
Mexicans are the largest immigrant group in the United States, but their numbers declined by more than 500,000 between 2007 and 2024, according to a Washington, D.C.-based think tank that specializes in migration issues.

In a report published last week, the Migration Policy Institute (MPI) said that during “the past four and a half decades, the size of the Mexican-born population increased fivefold, from 2.2 million in 1980 to an estimated 11.1 million in 2024.”

There are many fewer Mexican immigrants in the U.S. now than there used to be. We analyze the changing shape of the Mexican immigrant population in our new article: https://t.co/wziuFZMd6W pic.twitter.com/v59T1RzSKl — MigrationPolicy Inst (@MigrationPolicy) July 16, 2026

“However,” the think tank added, “the number has declined slightly, from a peak of more than 11.7 million in 2007.”

Still, per the 2024 estimate, Mexicans accounted for 22% of the total U.S. immigrant population in 2024, which was 50.2 million, according to MPI.

The exact numbers in the MPI report showed that the number of Mexican-born U.S. residents fell by 567,000 between 2007 and 2024.

The think tank said that “future declines in the Mexican immigrant population may accelerate due to heightened immigration enforcement at the U.S.-Mexico border and within the U.S. interior,” where the Trump administration is carrying out an aggressive deportation agenda.

“Authorities’ encounters of migrants of all nationalities crossing the southern border without authorization fell to about 238,000 in fiscal year (FY) 2025 — the lowest level in 55 years and a sharp departure from post-2021 patterns in which annual encounters consistently exceeded 1 million,” MPI said.

“Mexicans represented 47 percent of those FY 2025 unauthorized crossings, epitomizing the significant diversification in flows arriving at the border since the early 2000s, before which Mexican crossings dominated.”

Among the Mexican-born population of the United States, around one-third to one-half are potentially vulnerable to deportation. In a 2024 report, BBVA research put the number of Mexicans in the U.S. at 12 million. The Spanish bank’s research division said that 4.1 million of that number were undocumented.

However, in its report, MPI said it estimated that “about 5.5 million unauthorized immigrants were from Mexico as of mid-2023.”

That number is just under 50% of the 11.1 million Mexican-born U.S. residents in 2024, per MPI’s numbers.

Citing data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey, MPI said that “an estimated 40.5 million U.S. residents traced their ancestry or heritage to Mexico.” That includes people born in Mexico and people born in the U.S. or elsewhere, MPI said.

A profile of Mexicans in the US

MPI said that Mexican immigrants in the United States “are concentrated in a handful of states and metropolitan areas.”

It said that between 2020 and 2024, 70% of all Mexicans who lived in the U.S. were concentrated in five states: California (35%); Texas (22%); Illinois (6%); Arizona (5%); and Florida (2%).

“During the same period, close to 35 percent of Mexican immigrants lived in one of five greater metropolitan areas: Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston, Dallas, and Riverside,” MPI said.

The think tank also said that Mexican immigrants in the U.S. “have relatively low average educational attainment and income but a high labor-force participation rate and are especially likely to be of working age.”

MPI said that in 2024:

The median age of Mexican immigrants in the U.S. was 47, “which equaled that of the overall foreign-born population but was higher than that of the U.S. born (37).”

Just 10% of Mexican immigrant adults (ages 25 and older) held a bachelor’s degree or higher, compared to 36% of all immigrants and 37% of the U.S.-born population.

49% of Mexican immigrant adults lacked a high school diploma.

About 65% of Mexican immigrants aged 5 and older reported speaking English less than “very well,” compared to 47% of all immigrants.

Mexican immigrants had a civilian labor-force participation rate of 68%, equal to that of the overall foreign-born population and higher than the U.S.-born population (63%).

Mexican immigrants with jobs were primarily working in services (26%), followed by natural resources, construction, and maintenance (25%) and production, transport and material moving (20%).

Mexican immigrants had a median household income of US $68,700, below the median incomes of immigrant households overall ($82,400) and U.S.-born-led households ($81,400).

Approximately 16% of Mexican immigrants were living in poverty, slightly higher than rates for the overall foreign-born population (14%) and the U.S.-born population (12%).

Around 34% of Mexican immigrants were U.S. citizens, compared to 51% of immigrants overall, while many more Mexicans were lawful permanent residents of the United States.

About 77% of Mexicans arrived in the United States prior to 2010, “making this a long-settled population.”

At her Thursday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum noted that her sister has lived in the United States for more than 30 years.

“As is the case with my family, I think all Mexicans have a close or distant relative who lives in the United States,” she said.

“That link” between Mexico and the United States “will never be broken,” Sheinbaum added.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: Mexico’s inflation falls to its lowest level since 2020
World.content:
Inflation in Mexico moderated again during the first half of July — the eighth consecutive 15-day period in which the rate declined — settling close to the Bank of Mexico’s target.

The national statistics institute INEGI on Thursday reported that the National Consumer Price Index rose 0.07% compared to the second half of June, bringing the annual headline inflation rate to 3.10%. This is the lowest for any quincena, as the half-month period is known, since the second half of December 2020.

The data reflected a slowdown compared to the 3.37% annual rate recorded for the month of June. It also compared favorably on an annual basis. During the first quincena of July 2025, the bi-weekly inflation rate was 0.15% and the annual rate was 3.55%.

INEGI found that the smaller price increase in early July was mainly related to the behavior of the non-core component, which includes volatile prices such as agricultural products, energy and government-regulated tariffs.

This index decreased by 0.23% during the quincena and registered a growth of just 0.21% compared to the same period last year.

Prices for agricultural products fell 0.57% biweekly and accumulated a year-on-year drop of 3.53%. Within this group, fruits and vegetables decreased 1.50% compared to the second half of June.

Tomatoes contributed the most to containing inflation, with a bi-weekly price reduction of 13.18%, while serrano peppers (5.17%), tomatillos (3.24%) and avocados (2.59%) also saw price decreases.

Core inflation, which excludes the most volatile food and fuel prices and is closely monitored by the central bank as a better indicator of the medium-term price trajectory, rose slightly to 3.95% year-on-year, up from 3.94% in June.

Within this component — which increased by 0.16% during the first half of July — goods prices rose by 3.52% annually, while services became 4.36% more expensive.

Processed foods, beverages and tobacco registered an annual inflation of 4.89%; tuition fees increased 5.95%, while the remaining services (restaurants, medical consultations, telephone and tourist activities) increased by 4.83%.

With this latest reading, consumer prices have moderated for eight consecutive fortnights, including four quincenas that hit the central bank’s inflation target of between 3 and 4%.

After its June 24-25 monetary policy meeting, in which it left the benchmark interest rate unchanged at 6.50%, the central bank indicated that it will await clearer signs that inflation is converging steadily toward the target.

With reports from La Jornada, Expansión and El Financiero

World.title: Mexico confirms 20 ICE death complaints filed across 8 US states
World.content:
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (SRE) reported on Wednesday that the Mexican government last week filed a total of 20 complaints with prosecutor’s offices in the U.S. regarding the deaths of Mexican citizens in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) or during ICE operations.

The federal government first announced on July 9 that it would file criminal complaints in connection with the deaths of 17 Mexicans, 14 of whom died in ICE detention centers since May 2025 and three of whom died during ICE operations.

President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Monday, July 13, that the complaints would be filed that day. Her administration is seeking thorough investigations into the deaths of all Mexicans who have died under ICE custody or in ICE operations.

In an “information note” published on Wednesday, the SRE said that on July 13, Mexico’s Ambassador to the United States, Roberto Lazzeri, filed 20 complaints “in the jurisdictions where the deaths occurred,” namely Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Missouri, and Texas.

The ministry said that eight complaints were filed with state prosecutors’ offices and 12 were filed with county prosecutors’ offices.

The SRE also said that on July 14, “the Mexican Embassy in the United States forwarded to the Department of Justice, through the Department of State, the complaint submitted by the Attorney General of Mexico regarding the 17 cases, along with a formal request to open the corresponding investigations and to provide an update on their progress.”

The deaths of Mexicans in ICE custody and ICE operations — including that of an 18th Mexican who was hit by a truck in Florida last week while running away from ICE officers — have occurred as the Trump administration pursues an aggressive deportation agenda. On numerous occasions, Sheinbaum has expressed her opposition to that agenda, and last week she said she disagreed with U.S. President Donald Trump’s call for continued immigration traffic stops.

“If there is a person who committed a crime, he or she must be pursued. But migration in itself shouldn’t be criminalized,” Sheinbaum said last Thursday.

Lazzeri meets with DHS and ICE officials

In its release on Wednesday, the SRE also reported that in meetings with officials from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and ICE last week, Lazzeri “conveyed the Mexican government’s concerns about conditions in … [ICE] detention centers, including those operated by private companies.”

The ambassador, who only recently began his appointment in the U.S., also “requested clarification on each case” of deaths of Mexicans in the detention centers, the SRE said.

After the death of Alejandro Cabrera Clemente in an ICE detention center in April, Sheinbaum said she had instructed staff in Mexican consulates in the U.S. to visit ICE detention centers on a daily basis to check on the welfare of detained Mexicans.

“They were visiting them once a week, but now I asked them to visit every day,” she said.

The Mexican government has asserted that poor conditions in detention centers in the United States and a lack of medical care for people in ICE custody have caused or at least contributed to the deaths of Mexicans.

Lazzeri also met last week with Michael Kozak, a senior official with the Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs, a division of the U.S. Department of State.

Western Hemisphere Affairs Senior Bureau Official Michael Kozak met Mexican Ambassador Roberto Lazzeri today in Washington. SBO Kozak returned Mexico’s letters that purport to direct the actions of U.S. Government personnel operating in U.S. sovereign territory. SBO Kozak also… — Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs (@WHAAsstSecty) July 17, 2026

After the July 17 meeting, the Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs said on social media that “Kozak returned Mexico’s letters that purport to direct the actions of U.S. Government personnel operating in U.S. sovereign territory.”

“SBO Kozak also recommended Mexico share its concerns [regarding the deaths of Mexicans in the U.S.] via diplomatic channels as is customary,” the post added.

Mexico seeks assistance from UN high commissioner for human rights

The SRE said that on July 14, Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco sent a letter to U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk “informing him of the events” — i.e., the deaths of Mexicans under ICE custody and in ICE operations.

In the letter, Velasco asked Türk to “consider gathering information through requests for clarification from the United States, analyze their compatibility with international human rights instruments, and make technical recommendations to help prevent incidents of this kind.”

In late June, the high commissioner “urged prompt action to prevent further loss of life in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody and called for independent investigations into all deaths under ICE custody,” according to a UN press release.

World.title: New rail lines will connect central Mexico to the Pacific and points north
World.content:
The Mexican government has launched the second construction phase of its ambitious passenger rail program, a phase that will connect central Mexico via high-speed trains to Saltillo to the north and to the Pacific coast to the west, as well as advance connections between El Bajío cities such as Querétaro, San Luis Potosi and San Miguel de Allende.

Speaking at the 25th National Meeting on Highway Engineering in Morelia, Michoacán, Efraín Deschamps Gutiérrez de Velasco, head of works at the Agency for Trains and Integrated Public Transportation (Attrapi), explained that the engineering and demand studies necessary for the next stage have been completed.

“We want to consolidate a modern rail system,” Deschamps said.

The second phase includes work on the Irapuato-León and León-Guadalajara sections, which will be built by the Felipe Ángeles Engineering Group – the same group responsible for the Felipe Ángeles International Airport near Mexico City.

Attrapi has also launched the international tender process needed to inject cost-saving competition into the selection of a contractor for the first section of the Querétaro-San Luis Potosí route, which includes the 68-kilometer stretch between Querétaro and San Miguel de Allende.

Construction for this section is expected to begin on Sept. 24, according to business intelligence platform Bnamericas.

Meanwhile, bidding for the northbound San Luis Potosí-Saltillo section will take place in stages between June and September, while the Mazatlán-Los Mochis section remains in the pre-investment study phase with no authorized start date for construction.

Finally, the Querétaro-San Luis Potosí route is part of the eventual Mexico City-Nuevo Laredo corridor planned for completion in future phases.

A third phase will expand high-speed rail service along 1,100 kilometers of the Pacific corridor, with routes linking Guadalajara, Tepic, Mazatlán, Los Mochis, Guaymas and Hermosillo. Plans also include a potential fourth-phase project extending this western network north to Nogales on the United States border.

According to Attrapi, the new rail lines are expected to operate at speeds of between 160 and 200 kilometers per hour and will be dedicated exclusively to passenger service, with no level crossings or interaction with freight trains.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: All about Oxxo, Mexico’s convenience store giant
World.content:
“A la vuelta de tu vida.”

Loosely translated, this phrase — the slogan of Mexican convenience store chain Oxxo — means “On the corner of your life.”

That is not much of an exaggeration: Oxxo stores are truly ubiquitous in Mexico.

For good or for bad, I live directly opposite one in Mexico City. There is another Oxxo store about two minutes’ walk from my front door if I want a little more exercise before I open my packet of chips or caguama.

As a news outlet focused on Mexico, Mexico News Daily has naturally reported quite extensively on Oxxo.

We’ve written about “Mexico’s coolest Oxxo“; the history of the chain and Mexicans’ “love-hate relationship with it; the “Oxxo diet” (that any reputable nutritionist wouldn’t recommend!); the chain’s expansion to the United States; and Oxxo’s long-term plans.

The list goes on.

In this “Mexico in Numbers” article, we’ll take a look at some key Oxxo numbers, including one that is the answer to a question you may have asked yourself or someone else: Exactly how many Oxxos are there in Mexico?

* The data and information in this article, unless otherwise stated, come either from the Oxxo website or from quarterly results reports published by FEMSA, Oxxo’s parent company.

How long has Oxxo been in business?

The first Oxxo store — created by the Cuauhtémoc Brewery — opened in the northern city of Monterrey, Nuevo León, in 1978. Therefore, Oxxo celebrates its 48th birthday this year.

There will no doubt be significant celebrations (and promotions) when Oxxo reaches the half-century milestone in 2028.

How many Oxxo stores are there?

As of March 31, 2026, Oxxo had 24,455 stores in Mexico, an annual increase of 3.8%.

Oxxo has stores in all 32 federal entities in Mexico. In addition, there are Oxxo stores in Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Peru and the United States.

The chain has expanded rapidly this century. In 2000, there were fewer than 2,000 Oxxo stores, according to the website Latinometrics.

Which states have the most Oxxos?

At the end of 2025, Nuevo León had 2,514 Oxxo stores, more than any other state, according to a report published by the newspaper El Mañana de Nuevo Laredo.

Four other states had more than 1,000 Oxxo stores at the end of last year:

Mexico City: 2,074

México state: 1,325

Baja California: 1,144

Jalisco: 1,075

On average, how many new Oxxo stores open per day?

The number of Oxxo stores in Mexico increased by 888 in the 12 months to March 31, 2026.

Therefore, the number of Oxxo stores in Mexico increased by 2.43 per day in the period. This accounts for both the opening of new stores and any closures.

How many products are available in an Oxxo store?

Oxxo sells “more than 2,500 products in all stores, ranging from chewing gum to cell phones,” according to the chain.

What is the gender makeup of the Oxxo workforce?

Have you noticed more women than men working in Oxxo stores?

According to the chain, six of every 10 Oxxo workers are women.

How many employees does Oxxo have?

According to the newspaper Telediario, Oxxo had more than 320,000 workers in late 2023, making it one of Mexico’s largest employers.

Oxxo said in 2023 that more than 2,800 of its employees were seniors, 900 had a disability and over 600 were refugees or immigrants.

How many people go to Oxxo on a daily basis?

Every day, Oxxo serves more than 13 million customers, according to the chain. In addition to buying snacks, beverages and household items, Oxxo customers can access services such as the withdrawal of cash and payment of bills.

On average, a customer spent 61.2 (US $3.50) pesos during a visit to Oxxo in the first quarter of 2026, an annual increase of 6.6%.

How much money does Oxxo make?

In the first quarter of 2026, Oxxo México had total revenue of 74.24 billion pesos (US $4.27 billion), an annual increase of 8.3%.

Profits in the same period were just under 5.63 billion pesos ($323.27 million), an annual increase of 20.9%.

How close is too close?

You’ve probably seen Oxxo stores in close proximity to each other.

But did you know that in the northern border city of Tijuana, one Oxxo store sits right on top of another?

According to Oxxo, each store serves a different residential area of Tijuana.

The numbers here? Two-in-one.

World.content:

Key Facts —The deal. Raízen closed the largest out-of-court (extrajudicial) debt restructuring in Brazil’s history, covering about R$64.7 billion (US$12.7 billion). —The backers. Shell is injecting R$3.5 billion (US$686 million), with a possible extra R$500 million (US$98 million) from the Ometto family’s Aguassanta. —The support. The plan won backing from 19 banks and more than 80 bondholders, with about 75% creditor adhesion. —The terms. About 45% of the restructured debt converts into equity; the rest is refinanced into new notes maturing in 2032 and 2034. —The point. The deal lets Raízen fix its balance sheet without a full court-supervised bankruptcy.

Brazil just saw its largest corporate debt workout ever, and it was struck without a bankruptcy court running the show. The Raízen extrajudicial recovery restructures roughly R$64.7 billion (US$12.7 billion) in debt, a landmark for one of the country’s biggest energy companies.

A fuel station. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

Raízen is a joint venture between Brazil’s Cosan and the oil major Shell. It is one of the world’s largest producers of sugar and ethanol and Brazil’s second-biggest fuel distributor, running the Shell-branded service stations across the country.

Like many capital-heavy companies, it borrowed heavily to grow. Then Brazil’s steep interest rates turned that debt into a burden, forcing a reckoning.

What an Extrajudicial Recovery Is

Brazil offers two main routes for a company in debt trouble. A judicial recovery is court-supervised, public and heavy, similar to a US Chapter 11. An extrajudicial recovery is lighter: the company negotiates directly with creditors and asks a court only to ratify a deal most of them already accept.

It works only when a large majority of lenders are on board. Raízen got there, winning support from 19 financial institutions and more than 80 bondholders in Brazil and abroad, with roughly 75% adhesion.

Inside the Numbers

The plan reworks about R$64.7 billion (US$12.7 billion) in financial debt, the largest extrajudicial agreement ever closed in Brazil.

Roughly 45% of the restructured debt will convert into equity, meaning some creditors trade what they are owed for a stake in the company. The remaining 55% is refinanced or amended through new debt securities maturing in 2032 and 2034.

Crucially, the controllers are putting money in. Shell is injecting about R$3.5 billion (US$686 million), and Aguassanta, tied to the Ometto family that controls Cosan, may add up to R$500 million (US$98 million).

Why It Matters

For Raízen, the deal buys time and breathing room: a longer runway to pay, a lighter interest load and the Shell brand still firmly behind it.

For Brazil, it is a sign of the strain that high interest rates put even on blue-chip companies, and a template showing other indebted giants a path between muddling through and a full bankruptcy filing.

It is a Brazilian out-of-court restructuring in which a company negotiates directly with creditors and asks a court only to ratify a plan most of them already accept, lighter and faster than a full judicial recovery.

Vista Energy just moved into a bigger league. In its Vista Energy second quarter report, the shale producer nearly doubled its cash flow as a major acquisition in Argentina’s Vaca Muerta, combined with organic growth, pushed production and revenue sharply higher.

Vista Energy is one of the leading independent oil producers in Vaca Muerta, the vast shale formation in Argentina’s Patagonia that has turned the country into a rising force in world energy.

Founded and led by Miguel Galuccio, a former head of Argentina’s state oil company YPF, Vista is incorporated in Mexico and listed in both New York and Mexico City. It reports its accounts in US dollars.

Its latest quarter shows what happens when a fast-growing driller bolts a large acquisition onto already-rising output.

Inside the Vista Energy Second Quarter

Total revenue jumped about 89% from a year earlier to roughly US$1.15 billion, as Vista sold far more oil into a firm price environment.

The headline number was cash generation. Adjusted EBITDA — a measure of operating cash flow — climbed about 99%, close to doubling, to around US$805 million.

Net income rose about 37% to roughly US$322 million. That was a record for the company, even if it fell short of some analysts’ loftier profit forecasts.

Underpinning it all was production of about 156,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, up 32%, with oil alone at roughly 135,000 barrels a day, up 33%.

The Equinor Deal Changes the Scale

The quarter was shaped by the closing of Vista’s acquisition of Equinor’s stake in a Vaca Muerta asset — a deal that, together with the company’s own drilling, lifted it to a new size.

Buying producing acreage is the fastest way for a shale company to add barrels, and Vista’s management framed the move as leaving it well placed to capture the upside if oil prices stay strong.

It also deepens Vista’s concentration in Vaca Muerta, the play that has drawn billions of dollars in investment as Argentina bets on shale to reverse years of energy imports.

Why Vaca Muerta Matters

Vaca Muerta is central to Argentina’s economic hopes. More oil and gas from the formation means more exports, more dollars and a stronger balance of payments for a country long starved of hard currency.

Companies like Vista are the vehicles for that ambition, turning geology into cash flow and, the government hopes, into a durable export industry.

Fast growth carries risk, though: heavy spending, reliance on a single basin and exposure to swings in the global oil price can all cut the other way if the market turns.

What It Means

For investors, near-doubled cash flow and record output strengthen the case that Vista has graduated from an up-and-comer to a serious mid-sized producer.

For Argentina, the numbers are more evidence that Vaca Muerta is delivering the volumes the country is banking on.

The question now is execution: whether Vista can integrate its new barrels, keep costs in check and convert booming production into steady returns through the ups and downs of the oil cycle.

Revenue rose about 89% to roughly US$1.15 billion, adjusted EBITDA nearly doubled to around US$805 million, and net income increased about 37% to roughly US$322 million, with production up 32% to about 156,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day.

The quarter was defined by the closing of an acquisition of Equinor’s assets in Argentina’s Vaca Muerta shale, which — combined with organic drilling growth — lifted production, revenue and cash flow sharply.

Where does Vista Energy operate?

Operating cash flow (EBITDA) slipped 6% to about US$171 million. —The bottom line. Nemak narrowed its net loss to about US$13 million, from a US$24 million loss a year earlier. —The deal. Growth was powered by the February 2026 purchase of Georg Fischer Casting Solutions. —The drag. One-off costs and currency swings in North America held margins back.

Nemak sold a lot more metal last quarter, it just did not keep as much of the money. In its Nemak second quarter report, the Mexican auto-parts maker grew revenue sharply but saw profitability squeezed by one-time costs and a weaker North American currency picture.

Nemak, based in Monterrey, is one of the world’s largest makers of aluminum components for cars and trucks, from engine blocks and cylinder heads to lightweight structural and electric-vehicle parts.

It was spun out of the industrial group Alfa and now trades on Mexico’s stock exchange on its own. Because it reports in US dollars and sells to carmakers worldwide, its results are a useful read on the global auto industry.

Inside the Nemak Second Quarter

Revenue climbed about 19% from a year earlier to roughly US$1.5 billion, up from around US$1.27 billion. Two forces did the lifting: a recent acquisition and higher aluminum prices.

Operating cash flow, or EBITDA, went the other way, easing about 6% to some US$171 million, on extraordinary one-off costs and unfavorable currency movements in North America.

The net result was still a loss, but a smaller one: Nemak trimmed its net loss to about US$13 million, from roughly US$24 million a year earlier.

The Georg Fischer Effect

The single biggest driver of the sales jump was the February 2026 acquisition of Georg Fischer Casting Solutions, a European casting business Nemak folded into its operations.

Deals like that quickly enlarge revenue, but they also bring integration and restructuring costs that weigh on profit in the first few quarters, part of why EBITDA fell even as sales surged.

Why the Margins Slipped

Beyond one-off costs, currency was the other headwind. A chunk of Nemak’s costs sit in North America, and swings between the dollar and the peso can eat into reported margins even when the underlying business is steady.

Higher aluminum prices cut both ways too: they lift revenue, but unless every cent is passed through they can compress the spread between what Nemak pays for metal and what it charges.

What It Means

For investors, the quarter is a bet on timing: the acquisition has already added sales, and the promise is that profitability catches up once integration costs fade.

For Mexico, Nemak is a reminder of how deeply the country is wired into the global car supply chain, and how sensitive that link is to metal prices and the exchange rate.

How did Nemak perform in the second quarter of 2026?

More than 100 works by Joan Miró are heading to São Paulo, some never seen in Brazil and some that never left Spain. The Joan Miró show is shaping up as one of the season’s biggest cultural events.

Joan Miró, the Catalan painter and sculptor who died in 1983, is one of the towering figures of twentieth-century modern art, known for his playful shapes, bold colors and dreamlike imagery.

Now a large slice of his work is coming to Brazil.

The Exhibition

Titled Miró: Mestre das Formas, the show opens on August 7 at the MAB FAAP in the Higienópolis district of São Paulo and runs until October 12.

It gathers more than 100 original pieces spanning paintings, engravings, sculptures, tapestries, photographs and historical documents, a broad look at the artist’s range.

Rare Loans From Spain

Part of the appeal is rarity: some of the works have never been exhibited in Brazil, and a number had never left Spain before this show.

The pieces come from the Fundació Joan Miró in Barcelona and the Fundació Pilar i Joan Miró in Mallorca, and the exhibition was made possible after years of negotiation and the backing of the artist’s grandson, Joan Punyet Miró.

Why It Matters

Major loans of a modern master’s work are a coup for São Paulo, reinforcing the city’s place as Latin America’s cultural capital.

For visitors, it is a rare chance to see Miró’s world up close without crossing the Atlantic.

A Life Poured Into Every Medium

Miró refused to be confined to the canvas.

His restless creativity spilled into ceramics, tapestry, and monumental sculpture.

The São Paulo show honours this breadth with photographs and documents alongside the fine art.

These archival pieces reveal a craftsman utterly devoted to the act of making.

Visitors can trace how a painted symbol might later reappear as a woven thread or a bronze form.

It is a rare chance to see the private studio practice behind the public masterpieces.

A Thematic Journey Through the Artist’s Mind

Curator Jordi J. Clavero has shaped the exhibition into five distinct thematic sections.

This structure guides visitors through the evolution of Miró’s singular visual language.

It moves beyond a simple chronological hanging of pictures on a wall.

Each section unpacks a different obsession that drove his decades-long career.

For Brazilian audiences, this offers a structured path into a famously dreamlike imagination.

The journey promises to make complex modernism feel intimate and deeply human.

Key Facts —The buy. Uruguay’s Air Force is incorporating six Embraer A-29 Super Tucano aircraft plus a simulator, for about US$100 million. —The scale. It is the largest aeronautical investment in the force’s recent history, contracted under President Luis Lacalle Pou. —The retirement. The move retires the historic A-37B Dragonfly after nearly 50 years of service, with a farewell flight in May. —The missions. Air surveillance and policing, border patrol, reconnaissance, close air support and advanced pilot training. —The context. Uruguay cites a regional environment of growing tensions.

Uruguay is retiring a Cold War-era workhorse and betting on a modern, combat-proven turboprop. Its air force is rebuilding around the Super Tucano, in the biggest aviation purchase it has made in years.

An Embraer A-29 Super Tucano. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

Uruguay’s Air Force has flown the same aging jets for decades. Now it is modernizing, replacing them with a turboprop built next door in Brazil.

The choice is the Embraer A-29 Super Tucano, a light attack and training aircraft flown by air forces around the world.

The Purchase

Uruguay is bringing in six Super Tucanos along with a state-of-the-art simulator, mission equipment and integrated logistics, for about US$100 million, the largest aeronautical investment in its recent history.

The first aircraft arrived in late February 2026, under a contract signed during President Luis Lacalle Pou’s government.

Farewell to the Dragonfly

The modernization ends the run of the American-made A-37B Dragonfly, retired after nearly half a century in Uruguayan service.

The farewell came in May, when two A-37Bs and two Super Tucanos flew together along the coast from Rocha to Montevideo before landing at the Carrasco air base.

What the Aircraft Will Do

Uruguay defined clear priorities for the fleet: air surveillance and policing, border patrol, reconnaissance, close air support and advanced pilot training.

Officials framed the upgrade as expanding essential capabilities like protecting the country’s airspace and borders in a region of rising tensions.

Why It Matters

For a small air force, the Super Tucano offers modern capability at a fraction of the cost of jets, a practical way to guard airspace and borders.

It is also another export win for Brazil’s Embraer, whose light turboprop has become a regional standard.

A Regional Standard Takes Root

The Super Tucano has quietly become South America’s go-to light attack aircraft.

Brazil, Chile, Ecuador and Colombia already fly versions of the turboprop.

Uruguay’s decision deepens that continental pattern.

It also strengthens a defence partnership with neighbouring Brazil.

Embraer’s design offers modern sensors and precision weapons at far lower operating costs than a jet.

For smaller air forces, that combination is transformative.

The shared platform could even open doors for joint training down the line.

What Comes Next for the Fleet

The first two aircraft touched down in February 2026.

Deliveries will now continue in phases through 2027.

Crews must master the new simulator before flying live missions.

That training focus ensures the force absorbs the technology properly.

Meanwhile, the remaining A-37B Dragonfly fleet will gradually ease out of service.

Uruguay’s air force is not just buying hardware.

It is rebuilding its entire operational backbone for the decades ahead.

Brazil’s Superior Military Court, the STM, must decide whether officers convicted by the Supreme Court over the attempted coup should also lose their military rank and position, a group that includes former president Jair Bolsonaro.

How and when it rules has become politically charged.

The Case for Waiting

According to reporting, a majority of the STM’s military ministers privately favor postponing the judgments until after the presidential elections.

Their argument is that a delay would reduce political pressure on the court and prevent the electoral campaign from contaminating sensitive decisions about the loss of rank and position.

The President’s Position

The court’s president, Minister Maria Elizabeth Rocha, struck a different tone. She said she will move the cases forward as soon as she receives the votes, with in-person judgments and no set deadline.

She stressed she does not intend to procrastinate and that the cases will follow due legal process.

The Coup Convictions

The proceedings flow from the Supreme Court’s rulings on the January 8 events and the broader attempt to overturn the 2022 election result.

Expulsion from the Armed Forces would be a separate, symbolic penalty on top of those criminal convictions, stripping rank from those found to have taken part.

Why It Matters

The timing question sits at the intersection of justice and politics, in a year when both are unusually raw in Brazil.

Whether the STM rules before or after the vote will shape how the decisions are read, and how much they weigh on the campaign.

What is the STM deciding about Bolsonaro?

The Superior Military Court is weighing whether to expel Jair Bolsonaro and other military figures convicted by the Supreme Court over the attempted coup from the Armed Forces, which would strip them of rank and position.

Will the STM rule before or after the elections?

A majority of the court’s military ministers reportedly favor waiting until after the presidential elections, but STM president Maria Elizabeth Rocha said she will proceed as votes arrive and does not intend to procrastinate.

Where do the cases come from?

They stem from the Supreme Court’s convictions related to the attempted coup and the January 8 events following the 2022 election.
