World.title: Las explicaciones de Zapatero dejan un sabor “agridulce” en el PSOE a pesar del cierre de filas de Ferraz
World.content:
El final del silencio de José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero le ha servido al PSOE para mitigar parcialmente el desasosiego que le carcome desde hace más de dos meses. El Gobierno y el PSOE han cerrado filas formalmente y aseguran que probará su inocencia, pero el sabor de boca que el expresidente ha dejado en su entrevista en RTVE, en la que ha negado su participación en el rescate de 53 millones de euros de la aerolínea Plus Ultra en la pandemia y no ha aclarado el origen de las joyas tasadas en 1,3 millones que guardaba en una caja fuerte en su oficina, empeora conforme se desciende en el escalafón socialista.

“Nos ha convencido”, sentencia un peso pesado de la cúpula del PSOE, donde la expectación “era absoluta”. “Confiamos en su inocencia, pero tenía que decírselo de viva voz a los españoles, que le escucharan, en este negociado hay que explicarse y lo ha hecho con seguridad”, añade otro miembro prominente de la dirección federal socialista. “Siempre es mejor dar explicaciones y dentro de lo posible ha salido bien. Ha dicho lo que podía decir, lo demás lo hará ante el juez”, piensa un ministro. “Es un alivio, pero me sabe a poco. Yo esperaba más”, añade un diputado del Congreso que “tenía toda la fe puesta en la entrevista”. “Las alturas dicen una cosa y la militancia piensa otra. Arriba se convencen entre ellos de que la entrevista ha ido bien y abajo, a ras de suelo, los compañeros siguen con las mismas dudas o más. ¿Qué es eso de que las joyas eran un regalo personal, que no le atribuya el valor de 1,3 millones y que lo va a someter a otra prueba? ¿Vamos a poner en duda también al Instituto Gemológico Español, que participó en la tasación [realizada por la joyería Ansorena]? Como mínimo suena raro”, advierte un miembro del segundo nivel del Gobierno. “Esa es la parte en la que más se ha tambaleado”, comparte un integrante de la cúpula del PSOE.

Pedro Sánchez no se ha pronunciado ni en el homenaje que el partido le ha dedicado en Ferraz a Manuel Escudero, presidente de la fundación Avanza, el think tank socialista, fallecido en marzo, ni después en el Congreso, adonde ha acudido para votar en el último pleno del curso político. El presidente ha dejado en el acto, que ha coincidido con el tercer aniversario de las últimas elecciones generales, el recado a Alberto Núñez Feijóo de que no debe verse ya en La Moncloa. “Cumplimos tres años de azarosa legislatura. Alguno el 23 julio se llevó un disgusto y no se lo ha sacado de la cabeza ni del cuerpo. Lo digo porque ayer [por el miércoles] escuché a Feijóo decir que sería presidente. Se le olvida una cosa: hay unas elecciones de por medio, y ya veremos”.

Sesenta y cinco días después de ser imputado por tráfico de influencias y blanqueo de capitales, acusaciones que el juez José Luis Calama de la Audiencia Nacional amplió abriendo una pieza separada por un delito fiscal y de contrabando por las dudas sobre el origen de las joyas, las respuestas de Zapatero han dejado “un regusto agridulce”, según el alcalde de una capital de provincias. La falta de concreción sobre la procedencia y el valor del ajuar le siguen resultando especialmente insuficientes a la decena de dirigentes territoriales consultados. Zapatero ha asegurado que las joyas no responden a un “afán patrimonial” y que se trata de “un regalo de cortesía, personal, de hace muchos años”. “En absoluto hay intención de defraudar [pero] Lo tiene que saber primero la justicia, hay que respetar los tiempos”, ha esgrimido. “Lo de las joyas no es nada convincente”, lamenta un secretario general autonómico, que ha visto a Zapatero “a la defensiva” y “obligado por las circunstancias.

Zapatero ha expresado su “gratitud” al PSOE, pero ha pedido que su apoyo “no lo haga por fe sino por los hechos”. “Con todo lo que he luchado mi vida por el Partido Socialista, que lo llevo a la sangre, sufro mucho pensando que el Partido Socialista pueda sufrir por la situación en la que me encuentro”, ha afirmado en la entrevista en la que por primera vez ha dado la cara en público desde que comenzó la investigación. “En la parte de Plus Ultra es donde ha estado mejor, pero con las joyas dichosas...”, apunta un senador.

Otro diputado cree que Zapatero “ha metido algo de reflexión y retrospectiva en el manejo de las joyas, lo que parece asumir un error pero no dolo”. La contundencia con la que el ex presidente se ha referido a ellas en un momento de la entrevista -“Me producen una alergia profunda”- ha sorprendido en las filas socialistas. Y ha suscitado más preguntas: “Pues que se las dé a Patrimonio Nacional”, observa un presidente de Diputación que concluye que “si bien Zapatero dice que no nos pide un acto de fe, en realidad es eso lo que está haciendo. Que le creamos”.

Los contratos de Whathefav S. L.,la empresa de las hijas del expresidente, por más de un millón de euros con Análisis Relevante e Inteligencia Prospectiva, de los hermanos venezolanos Amaro Chacón, son otro de los asuntos que más malestar, pero han sido las joyas las que han concentrado la mayor parte de los recelos dentro del PSOE. El “consuelo” de un barón territorial es que Zapatero “ha dado la cara”.

“Zapatero ya llega tarde, salió en ese vídeo que grabó acelerado el primer día y hasta hoy. No ha explicado todo lo que me gustaría pero al menos ha dicho que dará todas las explicaciones ante el juez”, opina un senador. “Tenía que salir, no podíamos estar en este impasse, lo necesitábamos”, zanja un dirigente con galones de Ferraz, consciente de la ansiedad que la investigación a Zapatero ha generado en toda la estructura del PSOE.

World.title: Implicaciones políticas, éticas y penales de las joyas que Zapatero asegura haber recibido por “cortesía”
World.content:
José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero anunció, tras ser imputado por un presunto delito de tráfico de influencias y ser registrado su despacho el pasado 19 de mayo, que pronto iba a dar explicaciones a los ciudadanos. No lo hizo y cuando, el 17 de junio, acudió a declarar ante el juez José Luis Calama en la Audiencia Nacional, le pidió más tiempo —“una semana o diez días”— para aclarar el origen de las joyas que fueron halladas en su caja fuerte en su oficina de la calle Ferraz y que un informe pericial ha tasado en 1,3 millones de euros. Tampoco lo hizo una vez expirado ese plazo. Este jueves, en una entrevista en TVE, es decir, más de dos meses después del hallazgo, cuando el periodista Javier Ruiz le preguntó de dónde habían salido, el expresidente del Gobierno se limitó a decir que eran “un regalo de cortesía”, pero continuó sin aclarar su origen. Eso lo hará, aseguró, ante el juez.

Zapatero insistió en que no hubo “afán patrimonial” alguno, pero lo cierto es que en el momento en el que no entregó esas joyas a Patrimonio Nacional pasaron a ser de su patrimonio personal. No especificó el expresidente cuándo los recibió, más allá de decir que fue “hace muchísimos años” ni tampoco de quién: “El país no lo voy a decir”.

EL PAÍS ha consultado a un magistrado, un catedrático de Derecho Penal y un experto en materia fiscal sobre cómo altera esa pequeña revelación —las joyas fueron un regalo”— a la causa judicial. El juez Calama abrió una pieza separada por posible delito fiscal y contrabando a raíz de ese hallazgo, que también tiene implicaciones éticas y políticas para el expresidente, que el PSOE ha defendido en alguna ocasión como faro moral.

Zapatero no ha aclarado aún cuándo recibió las joyas, pero el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, apuntó el pasado 18 de junio que fue en 2007. En una conversación con periodistas en Bruselas, el jefe del Ejecutivo explicó que habla a diario con el expresidente y añadió: “La España de 2007 no es la de 2026. Ni la legislación de hoy es la de 2007. Afortunadamente esto se ha regulado”. Pero en 2007 ya estaba en vigor el el código ético, sin rango de ley, que instauró el Gobierno del propio Zapatero para todos los miembros del Ejecutivo y altos cargos de la Administración General del Estado en 2005. El texto de la medida, publicada en el BOE el 7 de marzo de 2005, reza: “En el momento actual, se hace necesario que los poderes públicos ofrezcan a los ciudadanos el compromiso de que todos los altos cargos en el ejercicio de sus funciones han de cumplir no sólo las obligaciones previstas en las leyes, sino que, además, su actuación ha de inspirarse y guiarse por principios éticos y de conducta que hasta ahora no han sido plasmados expresamente en las normas”. Entre esos “principios de conducta”, el código especifica en el punto 3.6: “Se rechazará cualquier regalo, favor o servicio en condiciones ventajosas que vaya más allá de los usos habituales, sociales y de cortesía o préstamos u otras prestaciones económicas que puedan condicionar el desempeño de sus funciones, sin perjuicio de lo establecido en el Código Penal. En el caso de obsequios de mayor significación de carácter institucional se incorporarán al patrimonio del Estado, en los términos previstos en la Ley 33/2003, de 3 de noviembre, del Patrimonio de las Administraciones Públicas”.

Preguntado este jueves en TVE por si había incumplido su propio código ético, Zapatero respondió: “Será interpretable, como todo. Obviamente, como tantas cosas pasan en la vida, cuando la historia sucede y repasas, seguramente, hubiera tomado otra decisión en ese momento”.

El valor y el origen de las joyas

En un principio, Luis Arroyo, portavoz oficioso del expresidente, había asegurado que las joyas halladas en la caja fuerte del despacho de la calle Ferraz eran regalos y herencias con un valor de entre 30.000 y 50.000 euros. Tras el informe pericial que elevó esa cifra a 1,3 millones de euros, pidió perdón por haber “inducido a error”. Este jueves, Zapatero aseguró que ese valor “será sometido a contradicción”, es decir, que presentará un contrainforme pericial sobre el que ya tiene el juez Calama.

En cuanto al origen, el expresidente no ha querido aclarar todavía quién le hizo ese “regalo de cortesía”, pero Miguel Sebastián, ministro de Industria en la segunda legislatura de Zapatero, sugirió en un artículo en elDiario.es que podían ser de Arabia Saudí porque él había recibido en 2008 del entonces rey de ese país un estuche que contenía joyas de esmeraldas y brillantes. En ese artículo explicó que, tras consultar a su “oficiala mayor”, le dijeron que lo habitual era que esos regalos se los quedaran los ministros —lo que indica que ni los propios miembros del Ejecutivo conocían el código ético que habían aprobado tres años antes—, pero que finalmente había decidido entregarlos a Patrimonio Nacional y exponerlos en una vitrina del ministerio.

En 2007 Arabia Saudí condenó a seis meses de cárcel y 200 latigazos a una joven víctima de una violación múltiple por encontrarse con un hombre con el que no tenía parentesco cuando ocurrió el ataque. Posteriormente, el Rey le perdonó los latigazos. El Código Penal saudí también mantenía entonces la pena de muerte para quien mantuviese relaciones con homosexuales. El Gobierno de Zapatero aprobó la ley de igualdad en marzo de 2007 y la del matrimonio igualitario en 2005.

Tres escenarios

Los tres expertos consultados por EL PAÍS coinciden en que los posibles delitos fiscales derivados de ese regalo habrían prescrito y que si el entonces presidente recibió el regalo en España de manos de un mandatario extranjero no cabría el delito de contrabando.

Pero lo primero, destaca el magistrado Joaquim Bosch, de la asociación Jueces para la Democracia, es aclarar el origen de las joyas y ahí se abren tres escenarios. “Que Zapatero aporte documentos que acreditan que efectivamente es un regalo de 2007; Que Zapatero no consiga acreditarlo, pero el juez sí practicando una serie de diligencias: indagación sobre la tipología de las joyas, el fabricante, o incluso pidiendo esa información a las autoridades de otros países. O que ni Zapatero ni el juez consigan acreditarlo, en cuyo caso la interpretación más razonable sería la más beneficiosa para el investigado, es decir, la prescripción”.

Por su parte, Manuel Cancio, catedrático de Derecho Penal en la Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, explica que, si Zapatero demuestra que fue un regalo recibido en 2007 pero no lo declaró, “estaría admitiendo que en su momento cometió un delito fiscal, aunque ya no sea perseguible por los plazos de prescripción”. Al catedrático también le llama la atención que el expresidente reclamase más tiempo al juez para explicar el origen de esas joyas una vez que se hizo público el informe pericial que las tasó en 1,3 millones de euros “porque desde el momento del hallazgo en el registro de su despacho [19 de mayo] sabía que le iban a preguntar por su origen”.

José María Mollinedo, secretario general del Sindicato de Técnicos del Ministerio de Hacienda (Gestha), explica que los delitos contra la Hacienda pública (artículo 305 del Código Penal y siguientes), cuando la cantidad defraudada excede los 120.000 euros, prescriben a los cinco años en el delito fiscal y a los 10 en el agravado (a partir de 600.000 euros de fraude). Es decir, que estarían prescritos en caso de acreditarse que las joyas fueron un regalo de 2007. Mollinedo advierte que, en cualquier caso, habría que acreditar el valor de las piezas en el momento de la recepción y no del hallazgo. El técnico recuerda que fue el Gobierno de Zapatero el que en 2008, con la crisis, “estableció una bonificación del 100% del impuesto del patrimonio, motivo por el que se lo conocía como el impuesto zombi, aunque luego lo recuperó”. Además, la Comunidad de Madrid [donde reside Zapatero] que también bonifica ese impuesto, solo exige declaración de patrimonio a partir de dos millones de euros.

World.title: Amsterdam police chief pledges safety ahead of WorldPride
World.content:
Amsterdam police chief Peter Holla opened the COC’s Shakespeare Club at the H’ART Museum on Wednesday, telling dozens of drag queens and drag kings that behind the high heels and the glamour lies a great deal of courage – courage which, he said, “deserves admiration” and “deserves safety”.

The performers arrived by boat from the nearby Stopera, the city hall and opera house complex, at the museum’s jetty on the Amstel, where the ceremony was led by the drag figurehead Dolly Bellefleur.

The Shakespeare Club is a temporary community space run by the LGBTQI+ rights organisation COC Amsterdam. It runs until July 31 and opened three days ahead of WorldPride, the international Pride festival which Amsterdam is hosting for the first time from July 25 to August 8.

“We are a city of tolerance, but it is hard work to actually make that true,” Holla said in his speech, according to the Amsterdam broadcaster AT5. “That affects me and it affects us as Amsterdam police.” Some groups have a harder time than others, he said, and a day like this was a chance to show the force was there for them too.

Holla also set out what the police do for the community, including giving information sessions to refugees from countries where officers are, in his words, “a source of fear”. Officers from Roze in Blauw, the national police network for LGBTIQ+ people, join the Canal Parade as well as Asian Pride, the Trans Pride Walk, and the Trans Diner, he said.

He urged anyone facing intimidation or violence to go to the police. “Reporting is not easy, and many victims are afraid or just want to get on with their lives,” Holla said. “But we really need the information.”

Bellefleur said the speech showed what an unusual country the Netherlands is, because that kind of public backing from the police is rare in other nations.

World.title: “The Dutch are still alive and floating despite all this water”
World.content:
Originally from Venezuela, Eduardo Petit has lived in the Netherlands for over two decades. He currently works as a legal counsel in Amsterdam, enjoys the city’s beer bars, and would love to have Herman van Veen sing at his wedding.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?

I came over to study in 2004. None of my former bosses could believe that I was making the decision to go to the Netherlands. I still remember one of them asking me, “Are you really going to study law in a non-English-speaking country?” They didn’t understand at all. The Netherlands isn’t a destination for many people from Venezuela.

I couldn’t convince them or any of the other people surrounding me at that moment in my life, but I was convinced it was the right decision. I wanted to encounter a culture that was very different from my own and very attractive to me.

But I considered the Netherlands as my entry to Europe. I had no intention of staying here. Towards the end of my master’s, I thought about moving to Switzerland. I even studied French for it, but that didn’t happen, and here I am over 21 years later.

How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?

I guess I’m a staypat and a dreamer. A staypat is an expat who comes to another country and stays. I added dreamer because I’ve always dreamt that I’ll leave the Netherlands, but the deadline has never been clear. Perhaps there is a reason for that?

How long do you plan to stay?

I’m not planning to leave. I’ve never had a timeline, except at the beginning. Back then, I thought I would stay a few years. Now all these years later, there is no deadline. Who knows when I’ll actually leave? I guess time is wise and will indicate the path, but I don’t see myself staying here until I retire. I think I would rather go to a warmer place, which is my idea with my girlfriend.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?

I do, but I think that learning Dutch, especially if you live in a big city like Amsterdam, is a never-ending story. There’s still so much to learn, even if you live here for many years, because there are so many different ways to say things. There are street words and slang. That’s been my experience.

I took courses, but my best learning method was my personal relationships. I had a long relationship with a Dutch girl. If there’s one thing I have to be thankful for from that relationship, it’s that she was patient with me and with this process of learning. Her and her family really helped; just sitting there at the table with them and listening. After one or two years, I started to understand what was going on.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?

Biking. You can use a bike for everything here, even dating. You can ride a bike to the place, have the date, and then use the bike to get back. That’s pretty much my favourite Dutch thing, the ease of being able to pretty much live your whole life on a bike.

How Dutch have you become?

I’m now 46. That means I’ve spent about half of my life in this country. I tend to say 30% of me is Dutch. Why not more? Because there’s still a big portion of me that is international and that is Latin. I see and feel things differently. I see myself differently than the locals do.

As for the 30% that’s Dutch, I’m way more balanced with my views. I’m more concise and right to the point when it comes to business and virtually any other type of subject. I like to get to the point and there’s not much of that in the Latin world. In the Latin world, it’s more about storytelling. That’s what the conversations are like there.

People tell me I’m more Dutch, even my own family and Latin friends. I now really like planning. I’m not obsessed, but I like having a plan. It still eats at me sometimes because I love the spontaneous Latin way of life, but this is just how things work here, even on my weekends. Why do I have to plan everything for a weekend?

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?

Willem Drees. He was a politician and the prime minister of the Netherlands after World War II. The most important thing about him was the reconstruction of the country after the war and his social policies. He was a social democrat and one of his policies was to pool money and create the pension system.

He had a pragmatic view and realised that not everything was possible. He knew we could dream of a beautiful ideological society, but it could only be built slowly and step by step. I think his views and the way he went about his policies made him a very interesting man.

Herman van Veen. His voice made me believe that singing in Dutch can be beautiful. I never thought that was going to be possible, but then I heard his music. Another reason I would like to meet him is to invite him to sing at my wedding.

Johan Cruyff. He was a great footballer and a businessman. He helped build up the Barcelona club, but there’s also all the things he said. They were very simple and funny. I wish I could meet with him, have a beer, and just listen to him and laugh.

What’s your top tourist tip?

When I have friends visiting, I sometimes like to take them to the beer bars, but not the ones everyone knows about. I take them to the ones I call the hidden jewels, the small ones where there aren’t too many tourists.

I often tell people to get lost in Amsterdam or at least get out of the Red Light District. Go to Amsterdam-Noord, for example. It’s booming and there’s a lot going on there. There’s NDSM, the street art museum, and all the graffitti. It’s all amazing and different from other parts of the city. It has a contemporary landscape.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.

How the Dutch are still alive despite all this water and how they’ve kept floating after so many years. That’s something I admire. It all works because, here we are, especially with the old houses. I live in one of them in the centre of Amsterdam. For me, it’s amazing that we can live here with all this water.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?

I would go to the places where something interesting happened to me over these past 21 years. I would go check on the cinema I love the most, the Eye Film Museum. It’s beautiful and I could watch the sunset from there.

I would also want to go on a beer tour to all the places where I have great memories. In De Wildeman is one I would put on the list. Café In ’t Aepjen is another and it has amazing stories and history. I would also want to get some herring. I like herring, funnily enough.

Eduardo was talk to Brandon Hartley. You can learn more about Bucare Consultancy, Eduardo’s consultancy firm, on its website. You can also connect with him via his LinkedIn profile.

World.title: Rising costs force Amsterdam’s Kwaku festival to change
World.content:
Due to rising costs and regulatory pressure, this year’s Amsterdam Kwaku Summer Festival will be the last in its current form, its organizers have said.

“Kwaku is more than a festival – it is a unique social phenomenon that has traditionally meant a great deal to many people,” the organisation said in a press release, describing the move as a difficult decision.

“Stricter permit conditions, rising costs and increasing organisational complexity make it increasingly difficult to keep the festival affordable and accessible for everyone for whom it is actually intended. The organisation feels compelled to acknowledge that the balance in the current setup can no longer be maintained.”

“A shame”

“It’s a shame,” Zuidoost resident Alexandar Petrovic told DutchNews. “It’s a nice, big festival with great music and good times. There’s no money for that, but there is to buy F-35 fighter jets from the American military?”

Initially started as a football tournament in 1975 in the multicultural Bijlmer neighbourhood of the city’s Zuidoost, Kwaku grew into a festival with more than 120,000 visitors annually.

This year’s edition will go ahead as planned at Amsterdam’s Nelson Mandela Park in the weekends up until August 1 and 2. Featured acts include En Vogue, Kassav, Broederliefde and Dutch jazz legend Trijntje Oosterhuis.

Kwaku is consulting with local city officials to see if it’s possible to hold a different version of the festival in the coming years instead of closing down completely. Other festivals in the country are also struggling to stay afloat for similar reasons.

World.title: Unproven policy means less care for young women in crisis
World.content:
A growing group of young women with severe mental illness are getting stuck in the Dutch mental health system, and several clinics are responding by deliberately treating them less, an investigation by current affairs programme Nieuwsuur has found.

The women, estimated to number in the hundreds and aged between 15 and 30, have serious problems including chronic suicidal thoughts, self-harm and eating disorders, for which existing treatments are not working well enough.

Many are of average or above-average intelligence and struggle with perfectionism and a fear of failing or of not meeting social expectations, said Daan Creemers, a professor specialising in suicidality in adolescents.

When no treatment helps, several institutions turn to an approach known as Autonomie Bevorderend Beleid, or autonomy-promoting policy, under which women who ask for help do not always get it – including when they ask to be admitted. The aim is to break a cycle of repeated crises and admissions and give patients back control over their own lives.

“At a certain point you end up in a pattern in which we, as clinicians, feel held hostage,” Creemers told the programme, saying the policy is intended to return responsibility for young people’s safety to them.

There is no guideline for the approach and no scientific evidence that it works. The patients’ organisation MIND raised the alarm 18 months ago after receiving more than 100 negative accounts from people who said they felt neglected, and reported that in many cases the policy did not reduce suicidal thoughts and sometimes made them worse.

The parents of a 24-year-old woman from Eindhoven who took her own life in 2024, hours after being refused help at a clinic under the policy, have begun disciplinary proceedings. The case has not yet been decided.

MIND says it is not against the policy in principle, but that it should not be used until it is properly applied. The organisation has written to the health ministry calling for urgent research into the group. Creemers said the approach requires stable teams and the same clinicians over long periods, which staff turnover makes difficult.

If you or someone close to you is struggling with thoughts of suicide, help is available. In the Netherlands, call 113 or 0800-0113 (free) for 24/7 support, or visit 113.nl, where the chat service is available in English.

World.title: Highly contagious impetigo infection on the rise among children
World.content:
The highly contagious skin infection impetigo is on the rise on among Dutch children, with 2026 seeing more cases than in previous years.

For every 100,000 children, there have been a reported 350 to 400 children with the infection in the past three weeks compared to below 300 cases in previous years, according to research institute Nivel and based on data from GPs.

The infection, known as krentenbaard (currant beard) in Dutch, is mostly seen around the nose and mouth of young children, who develop red spots, bumps and blisters with a puss-like fluid that forms a crust when scratched.

The national public health institute RIVM advises parents to prevent their children from scratching the itchy and burning blisters and to have them routinely wash their hands with soap and water.

Impetigo, which is more common in the warm summer months, is caused by bacteria but can be treated with an antibiotic ointment. But because many people don’t seek medical help for its mild symptoms that often heal on their own, it’s difficult to assess how often it occurs.

According to Nivel, this year’s peaks coincide with the higher temperatures reported by the national weather institute KNMI.

World.title: Summery weather until Sunday, up to 29° in the southeast
World.content:
The Netherlands is in for a run of summery weather, with temperatures climbing towards the weekend before showers arrive on Sunday, weather service Weeronline said.

Thursday will bring clouds with the odd light shower, though most places will stay dry, and the clouds should break up in the afternoon to give some sunshine. Maximum temperatures will be between 18° and 24°.

Saturday will be the warmest day, staying dry for much of the time with sunny spells. A moderate west to northwesterly wind will keep the coast cooler, at 20° to 24°, while inland reaches 25° to 28° and the southeast up to 29°. There is a chance of a shower on the northern coast in the afternoon and evening.

Showers are expected more widely on Sunday, mainly in the afternoon, with temperatures back to between 20° and 24°. Next week brings a mix of showers and dry, sunny spells, with Monday between 19° and 24°.

World.title: Ali B cancels talk amid fears of media spectacle
World.content:
Rapper and convicted rapist Ali B has pulled out of a business event where he was supposed to be speaking on Thursday in Vinkeveen. The Missing Pieces entrepreneurial event has also been postponed until a later date.

“Due to the exceptionally large number of media applications for the Missing Pieces event, the evening is in danger of becoming a media spectacle. That is at odds with what this meeting is meant for,” reads a joint statement by the rapper and Missing Pieces on the latter’s website. “Therefore, we [Missing Pieces and Ali] have jointly decided to move the event.”

Ali B, or Ali Bouali, was booked, said the website, to speak about “why most entrepreneurs do not break through, despite their talent”.

But following Ali B’s three-year sentence for two rapes in May, including the 2014 rape of Dutch singer Ellen ten Damme, the resulting media interest made the event untenable, Missing Pieces said.

“The whole point was for the evening to be about entrepreneurship, without his personal situation being up for discussion,” reads the joint statement. “Due to the scale of the media attention, it is not feasible at this time.”

The activist group Dolle Mina had also announced a protest at The Harbour Club in Vinkeveen, where the event was scheduled to take place.

The 44-year-old rapper, who has denied all the charges, has appealed to the Supreme Court against the verdict – the highest form of appeal. Ali B has remained free for the years it’s taken his case to wend its way through the courts and will remain so while his appeal is ongoing.

Ticket holders will be able to attend the rescheduled event or get their money back.

World.title: Erasmus Bridge reopens after Rotterdam tram collision
World.content:
The Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam reopened to all traffic on Wednesday evening after the two badly damaged trams which collided on it that morning were lifted clear of the tracks, broadcaster NOS reported. Trams are running over the bridge again.

Fifteen people were injured, one of them seriously, when a moving tram ran into the back of a stationary one waiting for the bridge to close, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported.

The salvage operation took most of the day, with the trams having to be cut apart, RET director Linda Boot told the broadcaster.

Three investigations are now under way. Police are examining the crash, including with a drone team, transport company RET is carrying out its own inquiry, and the Dutch Safety Board has begun a preliminary investigation to decide whether to open a full one.

RET said initial checks showed the driver of the rear tram had not been under the influence of alcohol or drugs. He was among those taken to hospital. Boot said it was too early to speculate about the cause.

Rotterdam mayor Carola Schouten visited the scene and called it “a terrible accident”. No further information has been released about the condition of those hurt.

World.title: Poland appoints new human rights commissioner
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government’s majority in parliament has chosen Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram as Poland’s new human rights commissioner. She will take office after the five-year term of the incumbent, Marcin Wiącek, expires today. Gregorczyk-Abram is a prominent lawyer and activist, who is particularly well known for opposing the overhaul of the judiciary by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. PiS, which is now the main opposition party, strongly opposed her election, arguing that she is politically aligned with the current, more liberal government. Gregorczyk-Abram herself, however, has pledged to “put all my beliefs and views aside” when she takes up the new role. Senat wyraził zgodę na powołanie Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram na Rzecznika Praw Obywatelskich. pic.twitter.com/gz3rwGy3hi — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) July 22, 2026 The commissioner for human rights (widely known by its Polish initials, RPO) is appointed by a resolution of the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, with the consent of the upper-house Senate. Candidates must meet certain requirements, including not belonging to any political party and having legal expertise and relevant experience. As well as acting as a watchdog for human rights, the RPO also has the power to submit motions to the Constitutional Tribunal to assess the constitutionality of laws and to file so-called cassation appeals to the Supreme Court and Supreme Administrative Court against rulings by lower courts. Poland’s human rights commissioner has written to the government expressing concern that a "temporary" ban on asylum claims by most migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus remains in place after more than a year https://t.co/9SA2TypQdK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Gregorczyk-Abram was last month nominated as a candidate to be the new RPO by the main ruling party, Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), along with one of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica). PiS proposed a rival candidate, Adam Borowski, a veteran of Poland’s anti-communist struggle in the 1980s. However, critics argued that Borowski, an activist and former PiS election candidate, does not appear to have the requisite legal knowledge and experience. In a Sejm vote last Friday, the ruling coalition supported Gregorczyk-Abram, who won 233 votes to Borowski’s 177. On Wednesday, her candidacy was also supported by the Senate, with 59 votes in favour and 25 against, confirming that she will become the new RPO. Gregorczyk-Abram is best known as one of the founders and leaders of the Free Courts (Wolne Sądy) initiative launched in 2017 amid a wave of protests against the then-PiS government’s efforts to take greater control over the judiciary. Free Courts was prominent in efforts to defend the rule of law. Many of its leading figures are now associated with the current ruling coalition: Maria Ejchart is a deputy justice minister, while Michał Wawrykiewicz is a member of the European Parliament representing KO. In April last year, Gregorczyk-Abram was made chairwoman of a commission established by the current government to look into cases of abuse of power against civil society under the former PiS administration. In September, her commission published its first findings, in which it said that public media outlets under PiS control had “carried out systematic repressive and defamatory actions against activists, non-governmental organisations, and civil society”. Poland's public media “carried out systematic repressive actions against activists, NGOs and civil society” during the rule of the former PiS government, a report commissioned by the new government has found https://t.co/S2MO9KGssC — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2025 PiS argues that Gregorczyk-Abram’s previous activity makes her unsuitable as a suitable candidate for RPO, which is meant to be a non-partisan role. They also point to claims that she was involved in a group of legal figures that discussed the Tusk government’s controversial takeover of public media in December 2023. “[She] is a discredited and extremely politicised person who should be brought to justice, and not receive the laurels of the commissioner for human rights,” former PiS justice minister Marcin Warchoł told the Do Rzeczy weekly last month. After a Sejm committee hearing on Gregorczyk-Abram’s candidacy earlier this month, former PiS deputy justice minister Sebastian Kaleta criticised her for ignoring questions over her alleged “role in the illegal takeover of public media”. Zadałem Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram serię pytań o jej działania i możliwe spotkania z Ewą Wrzosek w sprawie przejęcia TVP, w tym możliwego tworzenia dokumentów prokuratorskich w prywatnej kancelarii. Kandydatka ostentacyjnie zdecydowała się ignorować te pytania. Ma bardzo dużo do… — Sebastian Kaleta (@sjkaleta) July 15, 2026 Speaking to state broadcaster TVP on Wednesday after her appointment was confirmed by the Senate, Gregorczyk-Abram declared that, “from the moment I take the oath and assume the position of commissioner, I will be independent and sovereign”. She pledged to “put all my beliefs and views – because each of us has them – aside and become an advocate for all citizens, regardless of what they believe in, how they live, or who they vote for”. Gregorczyk-Abram said that among her priorities as RPO would be the justice system, supporting the rights of disabled people and their carers, protecting older people, and fighting hate speech. With regard to the last of these issues, she noted that certain politicians present some groups as “enemies”, pointing to how this previously happened with LGBT+ people and judges, and is now being directed towards Ukrainians. Those are all groups who have at various stages been targeted by PiS and other right-wing parties. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: President to swear in new judge to Poland’s disputed constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has agreed to swear in a new judge to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), ending weeks of doubt as to whether the opposition-aligned president would accept the judge appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority. Although Sławomir Patyra will now be accepted onto the court, four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year continue to be excluded after Nawrocki refused to receive their oaths and the TK’s chief justice, also aligned with the opposition, blocked them from taking office. W najbliższy wtorek 28 lipca Prezydent Karol Nawrocki działając na postawie art. 4 ust. 1 ustawy o statusie sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, przyjmie ślubowanie od prof. Sławomira Patyry i tego samego dnia wręczy powołania czterem nowym sędziom Sądu Najwyższego. W przyszłym… — Zbigniew Bogucki🇵🇱 (@BoguckiZbigniew) July 22, 2026 Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK – for example when a judge’s nine-year term expires – the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again this week, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. Patyra himself has also made clear on which side of the dispute he stands. In an interview with news website Onet in May, he accused Nawrocki and Święczkowski of “blatantly unlawful actions” in deciding which TK judges can and cannot take office and suggested that the police should intervene. Sędzia TK prof. Patyra po raz kolejny zaapelował do Prezydenta o wyznaczenie mu terminu na złożenie przysięgi. Ignorowanie sędziego TK przez Prezydenta jest kolejnym przykładem psucia państwa. To pokazuje, jak bardzo siły anty-demokratyczne boją się odbudowy niezależnego TK.… — Dariusz Mazur (@_Dariusz_Mazur) July 21, 2026 Finally, on Wednesday this week, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, announced that Nawrocki had invited Patyra to the presidential palace on Tuesday next week to take his oath. Speaking to Polsat News, Bogucki said that, in the case of Patyra, initially “there were some doubts, but the president dispelled them”, without specifying what they were. In the end, they concluded that “we had a fundamentally clean situation here” and Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”, unlike the six new judges chosen by the Sejm in March to fill longstanding vacancies. “It was not President Nawrocki or the current opposition who destroyed and are destroying the tribunal; it is the government that is doing it,” he added. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. World.title: Germany deploys soldiers to Poland to help reinforce eastern borders
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Germany has deployed soldiers to Poland to help reinforce defences on NATO’s eastern flank in response to the threat of Russia. While Poland already hosts various allied forces, the presence of German troops is particularly symbolic given the two countries’ difficult history. “United, we will prevail,” wrote the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces (SGWP), announcing the deployment. “This is what allied cooperation looks like in practice, which translates into greater military readiness and strengthens NATO’s defensive potential.” Polscy i niemieccy żołnierze razem wzmacniają granicę z Rosją. Takie rzeczy możliwe tylko za Tuska ☺️ pic.twitter.com/oNBME2gBsv — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 22, 2026 Last December, the Polish and German defence ministries revealed that a “mid-double-digit number” of German troops would be deployed from mid-2026 until the end of 2027 to support implementation of Poland’s East Shield operation, which seeks to bolster defences along the borders with Belarus and Russia. They said that the German personnel would mainly engage in engineering work, such as digging trenches, laying barbed wire and constructing anti-tank barriers. Today, Poland’s SGWP confirmed that “several dozen” German troops, including “highly specialised engineering forces” along with their equipment, had since June been temporarily deployed to “support the Polish armed forces in expanding defence infrastructure on NATO’s northeastern flank”. It emphasised that the East Shield project is “purely defensive in nature” and comes in “response to threats stemming from, among others, Russian aggression against Ukraine”. While the armed forces did not reveal the location of the deployment, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated in a social media post that it was on the Russian border. Poland has a 210-km frontier with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle reports that the activities of the German sappers are focused in particular on improving defences around the so-called Suwałki Gap, a strategically important stretch of land around the Polish-Lithuanian border between Belarus and Kaliningrad. “Together, we are ensuring Europe’s security,” said Lieutenant General Alexander Sollfrank, the Bundeswehr’s operational commander, announcing the deployment today. “Through our engagement in Poland, we are strengthening NATO’s defence capabilities and underscoring the alliance’s unwavering commitment to ensuring peace through unity and credible deterrence.” Poland and Germany have signed a bilateral security agreement that will see the two neighbours and NATO allies increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity https://t.co/6BPX2WxvxH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 SGWP, which shared footage of Polish and German forces installing anti-tank barriers, said the work aims to “hinder and delay an aggressor’s actions in the event of a threat”, thereby “increasing the time for a response from the Polish armed forces and the entire [NATO] alliance”. It also seeks to “create conditions for the efficient reception, deployment and use of NATO forces on Polish territory”. SGWP welcomed “the involvement of the German contingent as a practical expression of allied solidarity and the result of consistently developing military cooperation between Poland and Germany”. It also noted that the cooperation would help the two sides improve their ability to operate jointly, including “developing the competencies necessary for conducting a joint defence operation”. However, it emphasised that the current deployment is focused on training and engineering, with no combat component, and that the German troops are unarmed. SGWP also emphasised that the East Shield operation remains entirely a Polish national programme. The leaders of eight countries on the EU's eastern flank have met in the first summit of its kind to discuss closer security cooperation. Finland and Poland announced that they would jointly lead an initiative, Eastern Flank Watch, to bolster defences https://t.co/fxRHpkM6w9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 The deployment of German troops to Poland comes shortly after the two countries signed a defence cooperation agreement in which they pledged to increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity. The agreement is a sign that the two countries now stand “shoulder to shoulder, as equals”, declared German defence minister Boris Pistorius. Poland is also currently seeking a new permanent US military base on its territory, after President Donald Trump recently pledged to boost American troop numbers. Last week, Tusk also announced that Poland will host military exercises involving France and the UK this autumn. Poland will host military exercises later this year with France and the UK to prepare for providing future security guarantees to Ukraine, says PM @donaldtusk. He also declared Poland's willingness to permanently host more troops from its European allies https://t.co/couian4FrP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland launches first of 11 planned “community forests” around major cities
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s climate and environment ministry has inaugurated the first of 11 planned “community forests” around large cities, with the aim of giving residents a place for recreation and contact with nature while also helping to fulfil the government’s pledge to reduce logging. Plans for the forests were announced in 2024, and the first has now been established around Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city. Ten other major urban centres, including Warsaw, Kraków, Poznań and Łódź, are set to follow. Dotrzymujemy słowa. Powołaliśmy pierwsze lasy społeczne w Polsce, to lasy ochronne wokół Wrocławia. Kolejne miasta przed nami. @MKiS_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/RxhsMZShj9 — Paulina Hennig-Kloska (@hennigkloska) July 21, 2026 “This is a historic moment and the beginning of a new approach to forest protection – with residents in mind first and foremost,” said climate and environment minister Paulina Hennig-Kloska at an inauguration ceremony outside Wrocław on Sunday. “Community forests are places where residents can relax, play sports and simply spend time close to nature,” she added. “At the same time, they are crucial to our security and quality of life: they retain water, regulate the climate, purify the air and protect the soil.” An area covering 13,000 hectares (32,124 acres) has been designated as a community forest around Wrocław. Forest management there will now be aimed at “maximising the forest’s social functions”, says the ministry, while timber harvesting is also restricted. The area will be divided into three zones, including “natural forests”, where nature will be left to take its course, and “near-natural forests” with minimal intervention. However, the largest zone, amounting to over 8,000 hectares, will be “social forests”, which the state forestry agency says “will be managed in a way that ensures the comfort of those who use the forest and its benefits related to wellbeing, physical exercise and recreation”. Hennig-Kloska noted that, in the latter area, educational trails as well as hiking and cycling paths would be established. However, given that such facilities already exist in many forests, it remains unclear how the new community forests will differ. The ministry is now conducting consultations and analysis on establishing community forests around ten other designated urban centres: Bielsko-Biała, Tricity (Gdańsk-Gdynia-Sopot), Katowice, Kielce, Kraków, Łódź, Poznań, Szczecin, Toruń-Bydgoszcz and Warsaw. On Sunday, Hennig-Kloska said that the “next in line” to have their community forests established are Kielce and Bielsko-Biała, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Shortly after coming to power in December 2023, the current government announced that it would halt planned logging in some forests. The former Law and Justice (PiS) administration had faced criticism for overseeing an increase in logging, especially in Białowieża Forest. The current government also launched plans to create Poland’s first new national parks in over two decades. However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed that move, arguing that it would “block the economic development of the region” and threaten Poland’s security. World.title: Poland joins EU satellite project developing European alternative to Starlink
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has joined a European Union project developing a secure satellite internet service that would provide an alternative to networks such as Elon Musk’s Starlink. Warsaw has committed €656 million (2.8 billion zloty) to the IRIS² programme, with the money coming from Poland’s EU post-pandemic recovery funds. In return for joining the project, Poland will gain access to the secure satellite communications network for government institutions, the armed forces and emergency services, while the growing Polish space industry will be eligible to compete for contracts linked to the development of the constellation Today Poland🇵🇱joins the EU🇪🇺space programme #IRIS² w/additional €656 mln. 🇵🇱 is on a remarkable space journey to build a strong space economy & secure connectivity for the defence of Poland, the Eastern Flank & 🇪🇺. IRIS² brings greater unity & strength for the entire Europe. pic.twitter.com/TwS59vpXtm — Andrius Kubilius (@KubiliusA) July 21, 2026 “This is a big day for Poland, the eastern flank and the entire European Union,” declared the EU’s defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, at a signing ceremony in Warsaw on Tuesday. “By investing in space, Poland is investing in its security, its economy and its future.” Speaking alongside him, Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said that IRIS² would help “ensure our security and strategic independence” while “demonstrating that Poland aims to be a leader in the European space industry and remain at the centre of EU security efforts”. “No single country is able to build such a [satellite] constellation so efficiently, which is why we are joining this major project – to be part of it and one of its managers,” he added. The IRIS² programme aims to deploy a constellation of nearly 300 satellites in low and medium Earth orbit, providing encrypted, interference-resistant communications for governments, defence agencies, emergency services and selected commercial users across the EU. First announced in 2022, the project is part of the EU’s efforts to reduce dependence on non-European satellite operators amid growing concerns over cybersecurity, hybrid threats and the resilience of critical infrastructure following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “It is super important for Europe to have a sovereign capacity, and Starlink will never do that,” said Eva Berneke, CEO of Eutelsat, one of the companies involved in the project, quoted by Politico Europe. The project is expected to cost €10.6 billion, including €6.5 billion in public funding and around €4 billion from private investors. IRIS² is expected to become operational in 2030. 🇪🇺 The IRIS program is Europe's replacement for Starlink. The constellation will consist of over 300 satellites to serve Europe alone. Security and sovereignty! Like Galileo, it could surpass its US counterpart. Fewer satellites, smarter coverage. Eventually more could be added pic.twitter.com/Uswmuotw7F — Mariska den Eelden 🇪🇺🇳🇱 (@eeldenden) February 22, 2025 As part of its contribution to IRIS², Poland will finance six large satellites in medium Earth orbit (MEO) and six smaller satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO). It will also build a ground gateway station in Warsaw to connect the satellites with GovNet, the country’s secure government fibre-optic communications network. Earlier this year, the Polish government approved the use of money from its share of the EU’s post-pandemic reconstruction fund to cover its contribution to IRIS². Sięgamy gwiazd!! Polska przystępuje do europejskiego programu budowy bezpiecznej łączności satelitarnej 🛰️📡! W ten sposób zaspokoimy wszystkie potrzeby łączności służb i administracji państwowej. IRIS² zapewni nam bezpieczeństwo i niezależność. Dziękuję @KubiliusA za współpracę pic.twitter.com/c8u2QH0Wyn — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) July 21, 2026 Once the system is up and running, Poland’s police, border guards and other emergency services would be able to use the network during natural disasters, power outages and other emergencies when terrestrial communications infrastructure is unavailable. The system would also make it possible to provide temporary connectivity for civilians through emergency hotspots, says Poland’s interior ministry. Polish companies will now also be able to compete for contracts covering satellite manufacturing, telecommunications equipment, software and ground infrastructure, expanding the country’s role in Europe’s space industry. “It is estimated that each zloty invested in the project will generate a five-zloty return through new jobs, innovation and the development of domestic technologies,” the ministry said in a statement. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector. Last week, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that it will open a new security centre in Warsaw. One of its areas of operation will be satellite communication, including the use of satellite imagery to monitor critical incidents such as natural disasters. Prime Minister Donald Tusk also revealed that Poland and the ESA are working on the first Polish spacecraft, which would provide servicing, refuelling and other services for satellites Last year, Poland launched its first national military satellite. A Polish firm, Creotech Instruments, signed Poland’s largest ever contract with the ESA, a €52 million deal to build and launch a constellation of Earth observation satellites. Astronaut @astro_slawosz's recent trip to the International Space Station highlighted the Polish space industry's growing importance. Once limited to making components for others, Poland is now building its own spacecraft and participating in missions https://t.co/TmQiD91IzZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today. World.title: Kraków launches €43m “pre-design” tender for planned metro system
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". But his rival in next month's elections says the mayor is digging up forgotten plans as part of the campaign https://t.co/lg3zkNeW2E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2024 Rafał Solecki, head of Kraków’s department of strategy and European funds, also made clear last week that “construction of the metro exceeds the financial capabilities of the local authorities”, and that therefore financial support from the national government and the EU will be necessary. “The metro should be treated as a national strategic investment, similar to large railway, road, aviation and metropolitan projects implemented in other parts of the country with state participation,” he added. The city also announced that it has received a proposal for a consortium of seven local universities and research institutions to provide scientific and expert support for the metro project throughout its preparation and implementation. “Building a metro in a historic city is an extremely complex undertaking, requiring special attention to the protection of cultural heritage,” said Andrzej Szarata, rector of Cracow University of Technology. “Therefore, the support of the scientific community…is of paramount importance.” Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK. Poland says that the number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants over the border from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. “The effectiveness of [border guard] officers and the Polish armed forces discourages migrants from taking risks,” says Poland’s interior ministry. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 Among the measures taken to protect the border are a 5.5-metre-high steel fence as well as an electronic monitoring system that detects attempts to cross and dispatches officers to the scene. In 2024, following the death of a soldier who had been stabbed by a migrant attempting to cross the border, Poland also loosened the rules on the use of firearms by officers posted there. Since last year, it has banned asylum claims by people who cross from Belarus. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, also praised Poland’s “impressive” efforts “to stop illegal migration” and said that it was vital for the EU to offer financial and logistical support. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. She emphasised the “urgency” of protecting the EU’s frontier from the “predator” Vladimir Putin https://t.co/O9bhmLha44 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2025 However, while Poland has managed to significantly reduce the number of attempted and successful border crossings, there is evidence that Belarus has switched its focus to Latvia, another EU member state with which it shares a border. Last week, Latvian interior minister Jānis Dombrava told Euronews that his country has now “become the main target” for Belarus’s migrant trafficking, instead of Poland and Lithuania. On Thursday, Latvia recorded 111 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, compared to two in Lithuania on the same day and zero in Poland the previous day.
