World.title: Patriot extends Zambia copper discovery corridor to 5.5km
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Patriot extends Zambia copper discovery corridor to 5.5km Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright July 24, 2026 — 1:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Patriot Resources has put more meat on the bones of its freshly minted Tonic copper discovery in Zambia, extending the prospective geophysical footprint to about 5.5 kilometres while lining up two new drill-ready targets along one of the country’s better-credentialled copper structures. The company says its recently completed ground magnetics and induced polarisation (IP) surveys have stretched the exploration footprint southeast of Tonic, defining Blocks 1 and 2 as high-priority copper targets within the broader Mumbwa-Kitumba mineralised corridor. Patriot Resources recent maiden drilling has confirmed its Tonic copper discovery in Zambia’s copper-rich Mumbwa-Kitumba corridor. Patriot’s geophysical coverage now spans about 163 hectares supporting its view that Tonic may be part of a broader, multi-target copper system. Block 2 embraces an area measuring 600m square and is centred 3km southeast of the drilled area at Tonic. The target host is interpreted as a syenite – a coarse-grained alkaline intrusive rock - with high IP chargeability anomalies coincident with strong magnetic lineaments. Crucially, Patriot says the combination points to possible sulphide-bearing shear zones and the potential for structurally controlled copper-silver shoots.



‘With two new drill targets now defined, we are building a growing pipeline of copper opportunities alongside our recent Tonic discovery.’ Patriot Resources managing director Dominic Duggan Block 1 encloses an area of 700m by 400m, sitting a further 2.5km southeast of Block 2. It brings a slightly different flavour, sitting in a syenite-sandstone-shale setting with iron-rich alteration, quartz-carbonate veining and signs of hydrothermal fluid flow. The original Tonic target, along with Block 1 and Block 2, feature multiple coherent IP anomalies coinciding with magnetic highs and interpreted structures, with some zones modelled as being about 20m to 60m wide and extending to 160m depth. The company says the alteration style indicates iron-oxide copper-gold (IOCG) affinities, a tantalising piece of geological context in a region already known for that style of system. The mineralisation is tied to late stages of the Hook Granite, between 570 to 520 million years ago. Research by the University of Leicester and Ivanhoe Mines recognises the wider Mumbwa region as one of the world’s premier IOCG provinces. The latest geophysical work builds on Patriot’s early-July maiden reverse circulation (RC) drilling at Tonic where the company reported notable copper-silver-zinc-cobalt mineralisation from surface. One hole delivered 17m at 0.41 per cent copper, 4.7 grams per tonne (g/t) silver and 0.30 per cent zinc from 29m. That interval included 7m at 0.78 per cent copper, 5.1g/t silver and 0.38 per cent zinc from 30m.



The same hole also returned 3m at 1.19 per cent copper, 4.9g/t silver, 0.56 per cent zinc and 0.014 per cent cobalt from 31m, plus 3m at 1.06 per cent copper, 25.3g/t silver and 0.97 per cent zinc from 54m. The latter interval included a sharp 1m hit at 2.56 per cent copper, 62.3g/t silver and 0.76 per cent zinc from 55m. Patriot Resources managing director and chief executive officer Dominic Duggan said: “Extending our geophysics program from the Tonic discovery footprint has identified 2 new targets within the Mumbwa-Kitumba corridor. With two new drill targets now defined, we are building a growing pipeline of copper opportunities alongside our recent Tonic discovery, within one of Zambia’s most prospective and rapidly growing copper corridors.” Management says the Tonic system remains open at depth and along strike, with most of its defined IP footprint remaining undrilled. Importantly, the growing target corridor now steps southeast from Tonic for a total distance of 5.5km through Block 2 southeast to Block 1. The three target zones line up on the same northwest-southeast trending Mumbwa Fault Zone which hosts Sinomine Resource Group’s Kitumba copper deposit - about 18km from Tonic - and the Target H copper-cobalt prospect, 7km away. The Kitumba copper mine is a major greenfields open-pit copper mining project in Zambia’s Central Province. Its estimated total mineral resource lies in the range of 36 million to 48 million tonnes containing an estimated 675,500 tonnes of extractable metal. The nearby infrastructure angle would appear to not be lost on Patriot. Kitumba includes a processing facility and copper smelter due for commissioning this year, offering the sort of nearby pathway most early-stage copper explorers only dream about.



With Patriot’s phase two RC drilling and diamond drilling now on the menu, the company has moved quickly from encouraging first-pass greenfields results to a significantly bigger corridor play. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.content:
NationalWACourts Perth cancer doctor admits he made AI child sex videos Rebecca Peppiatt July 24, 2026 — 1:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An esteemed Perth cancer doctor has pleaded guilty to possessing and producing child exploitation material. Dr Peter Charles Swift, 68, was arrested last month after police conducted a search of his multimillion-dollar property. Dr Peter Charles Swift leaves Perth Magistrates Court on Friday. 9News Perth He was initially charged with two counts of possessing child exploitation material and one count of producing the same, but has since been charged with five more counts of possession after police continued to pore through devices they seized from his home. Swift worked at Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital and was formerly a consultant nuclear physician at Princess Margaret Hospital.



He specialised in general nuclear medicine, positron emission tomography and nuclear medicine therapy to treat benign and malignant thyroid disease, neuroendocrine tumours and lymphoma. Related Article Exclusive

Courts Former Perth hospital head of department behind bars, accused of making AI child sex videos During his first court appearance last month, police prosecutors said they seized 22 devices from Swift’s home that contained videos and photos of real and AI-generated children engaging in sexual activity. Those devices included multiple laptops, PCs, an iPad, phones and hard drives allegedly depicting category 1 and category 2 levels of child exploitation material. Prosecutors told the court there were AI-generated videos of children engaging in sex activity that Swift produced himself. Other videos found were of real female children under the age of 13.



Swift was granted bail a few days later and appeared in court in person on Friday, where he pleaded guilty to all eight charges. Swift’s lawyer Henry Sklarz previously told the court his client was a good candidate for bail because he was “a long and esteemed medical professional” and had “dedicated his life to the public hospital system, saving lives from cancer”. “He received national recognition for his work and is highly respected,” Sklarz told the magistrate at Swift’s last appearance. On Friday, Swift’s bail was renewed, and he will come before the District Court in September for sentencing. with 9News Perth

The latter interval included a sharp 1m hit at 2.56 per cent copper, 62.3g/t silver and 0.76 per cent zinc from 55m. Patriot Resources managing director and chief executive officer Dominic Duggan said: “Extending our geophysics program from the Tonic discovery footprint has identified 2 new targets within the Mumbwa-Kitumba corridor. With two new drill targets now defined, we are building a growing pipeline of copper opportunities alongside our recent Tonic discovery, within one of Zambia’s most prospective and rapidly growing copper corridors.” Management says the Tonic system remains open at depth and along strike, with most of its defined IP footprint remaining undrilled. Importantly, the growing target corridor now steps southeast from Tonic for a total distance of 5.5km through Block 2 southeast to Block 1. The three target zones line up on the same northwest-southeast trending Mumbwa Fault Zone which hosts Sinomine Resource Group’s Kitumba copper deposit - about 18km from Tonic - and the Target H copper-cobalt prospect, 7km away. The Kitumba copper mine is a major greenfields open-pit copper mining project in Zambia’s Central Province. Its estimated total mineral resource lies in the range of 36 million to 48 million tonnes containing an estimated 675,500 tonnes of extractable metal. The nearby infrastructure angle would appear to not be lost on Patriot. Kitumba includes a processing facility and copper smelter due for commissioning this year, offering the sort of nearby pathway most early-stage copper explorers only dream about.



With Patriot’s phase two RC drilling and diamond drilling now on the menu, the company has moved quickly from encouraging first-pass greenfields results to a significantly bigger corridor play. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Perth cancer doctor admits he made AI child sex videos
World.content:
NationalWACourts Perth cancer doctor admits he made AI child sex videos Rebecca Peppiatt July 24, 2026 — 1:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An esteemed Perth cancer doctor has pleaded guilty to possessing and producing child exploitation material. Dr Peter Charles Swift, 68, was arrested last month after police conducted a search of his multimillion-dollar property. Dr Peter Charles Swift leaves Perth Magistrates Court on Friday. 9News Perth He was initially charged with two counts of possessing child exploitation material and one count of producing the same, but has since been charged with five more counts of possession after police continued to pore through devices they seized from his home. Swift worked at Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital and was formerly a consultant nuclear physician at Princess Margaret Hospital.



He specialised in general nuclear medicine, positron emission tomography and nuclear medicine therapy to treat benign and malignant thyroid disease, neuroendocrine tumours and lymphoma. Related Article Exclusive

Courts Former Perth hospital head of department behind bars, accused of making AI child sex videos During his first court appearance last month, police prosecutors said they seized 22 devices from Swift’s home that contained videos and photos of real and AI-generated children engaging in sexual activity. Those devices included multiple laptops, PCs, an iPad, phones and hard drives allegedly depicting category 1 and category 2 levels of child exploitation material. Prosecutors told the court there were AI-generated videos of children engaging in sex activity that Swift produced himself. Other videos found were of real female children under the age of 13.



Swift was granted bail a few days later and appeared in court in person on Friday, where he pleaded guilty to all eight charges. Swift’s lawyer Henry Sklarz previously told the court his client was a good candidate for bail because he was “a long and esteemed medical professional” and had “dedicated his life to the public hospital system, saving lives from cancer”. “He received national recognition for his work and is highly respected,” Sklarz told the magistrate at Swift’s last appearance. On Friday, Swift’s bail was renewed, and he will come before the District Court in September for sentencing. with 9News Perth

World.title: Outdoor education subject saved from government overhaul
World.content:
Education Outdoors New Zealand says the government has changed its mind over the future of outdoor education as a secondary school subject.

It said outdoor education had been dropped from a list of subjects that would be developed by industry bodies ahead of the replacement of the NCEA qualification from 2028.

Instead the Education Ministry would develop the subject for study by students in Years 12 and 13.

EONZ chief executive Fiona McDonald said it was celebrating the decision because it would ensure the subject retained broad appeal to secondary students.

"The advantage of a ministry-led subject for outdoor education is it can be a much broader curriculum than just focusing on the skills and knowledge needed for students to go on into the outdoor ed industry," McDonald said.

She said it would lead students to all sorts of further study without necessarily wanting to learn in what she described as "a rather small outdoor industry".

McDonald said shifting the subject to industry-driven would have reduced schools' ability to deliver an outdoor education programme and fewer students would have been interested in the subject.

She said more than 3000 Year 11 students studied outdoor education and EONZ was concerned the government did not plan to offer the subject for that year level.

World.title: Cat stuck inside Wellington Uber's engine bay for several trips
World.content:
A cat took trips all over Wellington on Thursday, stuck inside the engine bay of an Uber driver's car.

Owner Renee Wadsworth said her cat Norton's tracking collar saw him travel all the way from Hataitai to Johnsonville - which was about a 30-minute drive.

She said Norton, a 6-year-old Burmese cat, had a love for anything warm and cosy, and he was also "a bit dumb".

Wadsworth noticed Norton was too far from home on Thursday, and raced to his nearest location to find him.

In Mount Victoria, Wadworth said she frantically looked for her cat and called his name.

She couldn't see him anywhere, until, she heard meowing from a car bonnet.

"I was honestly relieved because I thought that I was going to either find just his collar... Or I thought I was going to find his body."

After explaining the situation to the Uber driver who she said looked very confused, they opened up the bonnet to find Norton deep inside the car.

Norton at the moment of rescue. SCREENSHOT / SUPPLIED

"He was pretty shook up. And actually, so was the Uber driver."

Wadsworth called a local mechanic, who managed to squeeze the cat out via the front tyre.

"It looked like he was literally being birthed."

By Friday, she said Norton was perfectly fine, cuddled up on her lap.

Brendan Foot service advisor Mel Barrett said she got a call on Thursday afternoon about "a bonnet meowing" and rushed up to Mount Victoria.

"I've got nearly 10 years of experience in the industry and it's the first time I've had to get a cat out of an engine bay."

She explained the cat was sitting behind the front left fog light, away from any moving parts, with a plastic panel separating him from the radiating heat.

"He was quite well tucked away and safe."

World.title: Fiji's former chief prosecutor claims govt conspiracy to remove him
World.content:
Fiji's former chief prosecutor, Christopher Pryde, claims there was a racist, government-led conspiracy to get rid of him.

The New Zealand lawyer, who is in Aotearoa, spoke to Pacific Waves after corruption charges against him in Fiji were dropped this week.

Fiji's Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) threw out three charges in the Suva Magistrates Court on Wednesday.

A statement from FICAC said "the decision was taken because FICAC has been unable to effect service on Mr Pryde in New Zealand, despite attempts to do so."

"The proceedings concerned charges previously filed in relation to nearly $NZ150,000 in payments and reimbursements received during his tenure as Director of Public Prosecutions.Those allegations have not been determined in court," the statement said.

"Under section 49 of the Criminal Procedure, the entry of a nolle prosequi brings the present proceedings to an end but does not prevent subsequent proceedings based on the same facts."

'Bitter taste'

Pryde, aged 60, has always maintained he was innocent and said the allegations against him were contractual matters rather than criminal offences.

He has previously described the charges as bogus, politically-driven and designed to prevent him from returning to Fiji to prosecute an elite group maligned in last year's damning Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of Barbara Malimali as FICAC head.

"I am left with a bitter taste towards the current Fijian government and the Judicial Services Commission (JSC) because I don't think they have played ball with me.

"They made up their mind they wanted to get rid of me and they employed all sorts of tactics in order to do that," Pryde said.

Pryde claimed that the government's tactics were designed to intimidate him, and should serve as a warning to expatriates keen to work in Fiji.

"Unfortunately it is a salutary reminder to other expatriates that might be considering taking up a role in public service in Fiji to be careful." he said.

However he added that the dispute he had with the government and the JSC did not effect the relationship he had with the wider community, after living in Fiji for 18 years.

Alleged witch-hunt

The Sitiveni Rabuka-led coalition government's information director, Samisoni Pareti, declined to respond to questions by RNZ Pacific.

Pryde claims FICAC has accused him of evading diplomats who were sent by Fiji to serve him with legal documents.

"It's ridiculous, they know where I live, they've had every opportunity over the last twelve months to serve me," he said.

Last December, Pryde claimed the Fijian government committed an illegal act on New Zealand soil and sent foreign diplomats to stalk him at home.

"They sent people from the Fijian High Commission in Wellington to my home (in Christchurch) and harangued my neighbours by questioning them as to my whereabouts.

Fiji's coalition government continues to struggle at bringing democratic processes back after 16 years of dictatorship. (Supplied) ABC/Supplied

"They acted in an intimidatory way by staking out my home whilst I was away attending my mother's funeral," he said, adding that it was the subject of a formal and ongoing police complaint in New Zealand.

"The Prime Minister was made aware of this breach of diplomatic convention but chose to ignore it."

"The witch-hunt against me began when the acting Attorney-General, Siriomi Turaga, accused me of wrongdoing after I was seen with the former Attorney-General Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum at a reception at the Japanese Embassy in February 2023," he said.

'As long as iTaukei are on top'

Pryde was suspended on full pay for "misbehaviour" two months later and faced a further charge of receiving superannuation payments that had not been approved by the JSC in April 2024.

His superannuation ceased then his salary and all contractual benefits were "unilaterally" cut off by the Fijian government three months later.

"They (the government) want to get rid of me, it's all part of their ethno-national agenda," Pryde told RNZ Pacific in December 2024.

"Vulagi (foreigners) and Indo-Fijians are being replaced by iTaukei (indigenous Fijians).

"Hiring in Fiji is not based on merit, the government doesn't care, as long as iTaukei are at the top and in control." he said.

A tribunal exonerated Pryde on all charges in January 2025 and he was reinstated to the role, but he stayed in Aotearoa for fear he would be arrested on his return.

Several days after the Tribunal's decision, FICAC laid fresh corruption charges on him, including receiving a $NZ100,000 gratuity without the President's approval.

Wrongdoing denied

"I categorically deny any wrongdoing, the dispute was between myself and the JSC, whose chairman, the Chief Justice, Salesi Temo, tried and failed to convince the tribunal hearing that I had done something wrong," Pryde said.

"Issues around the payment of the gratuity were brought up at the tribunal and they were dismissed by the tribunal. So then we have a rehash of things into another format, they failed (with the charges) in the tribunal so they got FICAC to deal with them. That's not acceptable."

Prime Minister Rabuka criticised Pryde last July for failing to turn up to work, seven months after he was reinstated.

President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu then suspended his NZ$185,000 salary and benefits, following a public backlash over his absence.

Pryde said he had been living on his savings over the past year and was "relieved" that the latest corruption charges were dropped.

However he has filed a judicial review of the President's decision to cease his cut his pay in the Suva High Court.

World.title: Tornadoes, cold snaps, heavy rain and some sun: 'Every type of weather' forecast this weekend
World.content:
Heather Keats with details of this weekend’s cold snap Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Strong winds could close the Auckland Harbour Bridge this weekend, and a wintry blast of polar air set to bring snow, severe frost and icy conditions across parts of the country.

By Friday, weather watches and warnings were already in place for parts of both the North and South Island, including for snow on roads, strong winds and heavy rain.

A yellow Strong Wind Watch was in place for Auckland, with meteorologists warning Aucklanders could get gusts up to 100 kilometres per hour. NZTA said winds that strong could affect travel across the bridge for short periods.

The strong wind was expected to arrive Friday night, and strengthen into Saturday afternoon, before easing that night.

Motorists were asked to drive to the conditions and pay attention to electronic message boards on the motorway, which will advise if any lane closures and reduced speed limits are required.

About half-a-dozen homes flooded overnight between Thursday night and Friday morning in the Grey District, and there was a slip on a road on Cobden, with more heavy rain expected.

Weekend conditions will bring an icy blast, and could bring tornadoes

The heavy rain and strong winds could spark tornadoes in the North Island, MetService head of weather Heather Keats told Morning Report on Friday morning.

It could be an 'inside' end to the week' - at least for Friday and Saturday, she agreed: "Sunday's okay, but today and tomorrow, very much looking messy".

"We've got a bunch of fast-moving features and fronts tied up and that will be thunderstorms, snow, heavy rain, maybe even some small tornadoes and water spouts. And that'll race up and over the country - the North Island - tomorrow, and then it kind of races away.

"But then we're left with a very cold southerly flow. So we've got every type of weather coming over the next sort of 48 hours."

Thunderstorms had already hit Westland and Fiordland overnight, she said, with about 250 lightning strikes.

"Nothing crazy, but that's just the start of it."

On Friday morning, heavy rain was hitting Buller and Nelson Lakes.

A yellow Heavy Rain Watch was in place till midnight Friday for the Tararua Ranges, north of Wellington, with a moderate chance of being upgraded to a warning.

And more weather watches or warnings were likely to come, with tornadoes possibly in the mix, Keats said.

"The entire western coastline of New Zealand, I'm talking all the way up around Northland and the Coromandel Peninsula and then it'll track a little bit over to the eastern side as well.

"Thunderstorms, really strong wind gusts, and the conditions are right to see some water spouts and some small tornadoes. We don't say that lightly. Not all thunderstorms produce thunder, not all thunderstorms produce tornadoes. But we are seeing that signal in the models. So it's going to be a watch-this-space today.

"If you are anywhere sort of near those western coastlines, keep an eye on your app because if we do see a severe thunderstorm, we will put out that warning opportunity for you to get safe."

(file photo) 123RF

As for temperatures, among main centres Christchurch was likely to get bragging rights for the coldest, with it dipping below zero.

A Road Snowfall Warning was in place for the Desert Road, SH1, and snow was likely for Ruapehu, Keats said. While eight South Island roads had Road Snowfall Warnings in place, including Lewis Pass, Arthur's Pass, Porters Pass, Lindis Pass and Haast Pass.

Snow was also expected on the SH1 Dunedin to Waitati Highway.

Sunshine expected back for Sunday

"Because it's fast-moving, [the windy weather] won't be hanging around for long," Keats said.

"Once it clears out on Sunday, and we will have sun, we will have some nice weather coming for most of the country on Sunday, it just drops to be freezing. So we're talking -4C for Christchurch.

World.title: Some students in Dunedin asked to self-isolate amid flu outbreak
World.content:
By Patrick Manning, Massey journalism student

Some students at Carrington College Dunedin have been asked to self-isolate amid an outbreak of the influenza virus, with one requiring the attention of an ambulance.

A spokesperson for Hato Hone St John confirmed they were called out to Heriot Row, North Dunedin on the afternoon of 22 July, and sent one ambulance.

"One person was assessed and treated at the scene and did not require transportation to hospital."

A spokesperson for the University of Otago said the number of cases they were seeing was typical for this time of year.

"Only students who are experiencing flu-like symptoms in our residential colleges (including Carrington) have been asked to self-isolate whenever possible."

The spokesperson said at this time of year they expected to see more students with cold and flu-like symptoms and had well-established systems in place.

"This includes advising students and staff to stay home if they are feeling unwell and wear masks when in public, to practice good hygiene, and to avoid large gatherings."

Student Health Services gave flu vaccinations which were free for all Dunedin-based students and could be booked by phone or in person, they said.

World.title: Body found in West Auckland's Swanson believed to be missing woman Wolvnie Ding
World.content:
A body found in West Auckland's Swanson is believed to be missing woman Wolvnie Ding.

Police were appealing for information about the whereabouts of Ding after she was last seen in that area last Friday.

Acting detective inspector Megan Goldie at the Waitematā Criminal Investigation Branch said the body was found on Thursday.

"While formal identification processes are still underway, police believe the body is that of the missing 20-year-old," Goldie said.

"Police extend their deepest condolences to the woman's family at this incredibly difficult time.

"Family members have been informed and are being supported by police."

The police also thanked those who assisted in search efforts.

World.title: Man arrested after Wellington railway signalling cables damaged
World.content:
By Patrick Manning, Massey journalism student

Police have arrested and charged a man after railway signalling cables in Tawa were damaged earlier this month.

The investigation relates to an incident reported on 3 July, when railway signal cables were allegedly tampered with at the southern end of the Tākapu Road platform.

The damage caused multiple signal issues and disrupted rail services.

Police said in a press release on Friday afternoon the incident was a copper theft.

Wellington Police Sergeant Ryan Storey said his team executed a search warrant on 22 July but the suspect was not found.

"Our officers returned to the address the next day and arrested a man in relation to this."

A 43-year-old man was charged with intentional damage with intent to obtain a benefit or cause loss, and was due to appear in the Porirua District Court on Friday.

World.title: Former tertiary education staff pleads not guilty to sexual violence charges
World.content:
A former tertiary education employee has pleaded not guilty to sexual violence charges.

The man was given interim name suppression when he appeared at the Manukau District Court on Friday.

He is facing four charges - assault, indecent assault, and two counts of sexual violation.

His lawyer entered not guilty pleas on his behalf and said his client has elected a trial by jury.

World.title: Sam Kerr says A-League must find way to bring Matildas back, pay more
World.content:
A lot has been written and said about Sam Kerr over the years, but likening her to a Marvel superhero feels like a new comparison.

"I was really excited when I saw her coming on because I just had this Marvel moment where I was like, 'You have the Hulk," her teammate Midge Purce said after Kerr's influential cameo off the bench in her second game for her new club, which saw it come from 0-2 down to win 3-2.

"Like you thought this was everything and no, we're bringing on the Hulk."

A DC Comics-inspired reference might have been more apt considering she is now playing for Gotham FC, but whether she is Hulk, Batman, or any other fictional crime fighter, Kerr is already back lighting up the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL).

And she hasn't even scored yet.

Kerr made her Gotham FC debut last week. She used to play for the team under its previous banner, Sky Blue FC. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

The Matildas captain opted to resume her career in the USA's top domestic league, after a hugely successful six and a half years with Chelsea in England's Women's Super League (WSL).

"I didn't really see myself starting fresh at a new European club. Coming back to the US has always been something that I wanted to do," Kerr told ABC Sport.

"Being close to [wife Kristie Mewis'] family and just coming back and hopefully winning some trophies.

"I felt like I'd achieved almost everything that I wanted to with Chelsea. So it was just time for change."

A-League Women needs more investment

When it became clear that Kerr was leaving Chelsea, there were some optimists hoping she might return home to Perth Glory in the A-League Women (ALW).

But that is incredibly unlikely while the league remains in its current semi-professional state.

Loading Instagram content

"We need to find a way to get all the best players back," Kerr said, urging greater investment in the Australian women's domestic game.

"If it paid enough and it was a top league, a lot of us Matildas would go back, but to better ourselves for the national team, we have to go overseas.

"I think the A-League was thriving, or the W-League back then was thriving when the national team players and players from the NWSL, players from England were coming over, and whether it was a guest stint or playing, you had the best players in the league, week in, week out, training with our future generation.

"I think the A-League's probably more similar to the NWSL. It's more transitional, probably on the same level as the NWSL off the pitch with things like that.

"But I think the A-League probably needs a little bit more investment, a little bit more time."

Kerr said most Matildas players have to go overseas to further their careers. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Kerr's thoughts reflect broader concerns from players, who have repeatedly spoken out about pay in the ALW, which is the lowest amongst Australia's major women's domestic competitions.

It was not so long ago that the NWSL and ALW, or W-League as it was known, were seen as two of the leading leagues in the world, as players split their time between both.

Now Kerr and goalkeeper Mackenzie Arnold are the only regular Matildas playing in the USA; a handful of others are based in Australia, with most opting to play in Europe.

American league growing

While the ALW has fallen well down the pecking order, the NWSL is now jostling for top billing alongside the WSL.

The NWSL was founded in 2013 with eight teams and now has 16 and has experienced significant commercial growth, exemplified when USA forward Trinity Rodman signed a three-year deal with Washington Spirit reportedly worth $2.86 million a year, making her one of the highest paid female footballers in the world.

Loading...

Gotham is the reigning NWSL champion, and in a huge next chapter, in 2028 will move from its base in New Jersey to a new purpose-built football stadium in Queens, shared alongside Major League Soccer's New York City FC.

Kerr's debut came off the bench in the team's win over Washington last week, which was played at the home of the New York Mets in front of more than 42,000 fans, a record for a women's sport event in New York City.

The home of Major League Baseball's New York Mets hosted Gotham FC's historic game, where Kerr made her club debut. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

A few days later, her second game was a much more low-key affair, playing at a field enveloped by an athletics track, in front of several thousand fans who braved a 2 and a half hour weather delay.

For Kerr, 32, who had played for Gotham FC under its previous iteration as Sky Blue FC, the contrast in her first two games is emblematic of where the league is at.

"It's obviously changed a bit, but a lot has stayed the same too," she said.

"The fans and the stadiums that we're playing in now are what I think we should be playing in.

"And there's always been a lot of fun over here and a lot of excitement about the game, but in so many ways it still feels like the same league."

Kerr said the different styles of football in the NWSL and WSL make them difficult to compare.

Kerr has spent extended periods playing in the ALW, NWSL, and WSL. (Getty Images: Leila Coker/WSL)

"I think everyone's fighting for the top spot in the league, even in men's football, but I don't think it's worth putting my two cents in.

"I love both leagues, but yes, such different games in both countries."

Kerr's teammate, Ireland international Denise O'Sullivan, is another new acquisition for Gotham FC.

"I think it's the best league in the world; we've world-class players in every single team in this league," she said.

"And I think really the best thing about this league is the competitiveness from top to bottom. I don't think you can go into any game not right in it."

Kerr fandom high

Kerr's return is a major talking point for the NWSL and Gotham FC fans.

Amongst the crowd at her second game, there are already several fans sporting newly minted Kerr number 20 jerseys.

The Matildas captain is well known in the global women's football fanbase. (Getty Images: FIFA/Hassan Omar Wamwayi)

"Ecstatic! She's a blue; I'm a Chelsea fan, Gotham fan, so that collaboration, it just works together, I love it," Will from Jersey City said.

Teresa from Brooklyn said she was happy to see Kerr back with the New York-New Jersey-based club.

"Sam has been gone from the league for six and a half years, and we still see her name at the top of the NWSL scoring record. So if any NWSL fan doesn't know her, that's on them," she said.

There's even an eight-year-old girl named, what else but Matilda, or Tilly, who is there with her parents, having just moved to New York from Sydney.

"We love Sam Kerr and we're so excited that this is her team now, our home team is Sam Kerr's new team, super excited," her mum Kiki said.

Kerr is Australia's all-time leading goalscorer. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Not many Australians playing abroad attract this level of fandom, but even as she enters the latter stages of her career, Kerr still has the cachet amongst women's football fans here.

And she will be hoping her form can continue as she eyes off leading the Matildas to next year's Women's World Cup in Brazil.

World.title: Modra's medical records allegedly inappropriately accessed by SA Health staff
World.content:
Three South Australian health staff are being investigated for alleged inappropriate access to the private medical records of AFL star Tony Modra, who suffered serious injuries in a truck crash last month.

SA Health said another five employees were also being "assessed" to determine whether their access to the records "was always appropriate".

While the health department has apologised to Modra's family "for any distress caused", Acting Health Minister Chris Picton described the matter as "concerning".

"Where we do identify somebody who has done the wrong thing, we need to make sure that action is taken," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"People have lost their jobs for this before."

A close-up of the windscreen on the truck Modra was driving at the time of the crash. (Supplied: 9News Adelaide)

Modra underwent facial surgery and was in hospital for days after the crash at Back Valley, near Victor Harbor on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula, in June.

On Instagram, earlier this week the Crows legend posted an update of his progress, saying he was now able to get "out and about", and shared photos of himself in intensive care and recovering with his family.

The alleged SA Health breach is not the first time that concerns have been raised about hospital staff inappropriately accessing patient records in cases involving high-profile individuals.

A photo of Modra with family a month after the crash. (Instagram: tonymodraofficial)

In 2016, 13 hospital staff were sanctioned after being caught snooping on the medical records of Cy Walsh, who was charged with the stabbing murder of his father — Crows coach Phil Walsh — before being found not guilty by reason of mental incompetence.

In 2024, ABC News revealed an SA Health investigation had found 18 staff engaged in misconduct or inappropriately accessed the medical records of a patient understood to be Charlie Stevens, the late son of SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens.

Mr Picton was asked about how the alleged breach relating to Modra's records had come to the attention of authorities, and replied that he could not "exactly give you all the details, but I'm happy to check".

Modra shared a photo on Instagram of him in intensive care. (Instagram: tonymodraofficial)

"Because of the way we've got tracking of the system now, we can see every time someone's logged in, every case that people have looked at, and that's why we're able to know and able to investigate these things," he said.

" The very, very small percentage of people who would seek to do such a thing — they can be caught. "

In a statement, SA Health said it regularly conducted audits "to ensure that staff are accessing appropriate information".

"As a result of a standard audit, three staff are currently under investigation for potential inappropriate access of a SAHLN patient's record. Another five employees are being assessed to ensure their access was always appropriate," the statement said.

"Any staff member who has accessed information inappropriately may be subject to disciplinary processes, which may include termination of their employment.

"Our sincerest apologies go to the family for any distress caused."

SA Health Minister Chris Picton says the majority of staff do the right thing. (ABC News)

Opposition spokesperson Ben Hood said the latest revelation strengthened the case for an inquiry into patient record privacy breaches.

"It's deeply concerning that this again has happened in SA Health. It's a case of the 'standard you walk past is the standard you accept'," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"There is obviously an issue of culture in the department and the government with regards to this, and we think there needs to be an inquiry into it."

The truck Modra was driving at the time of the crash in June. (Supplied: 9News Adelaide)

Premier Peter Malinauskas said the alleged breach was a "disappointing development" but that the "overall majority" of the SA Health workforce, which he said numbered 50,000, did the right thing.

"It's unfortunate that a few individuals here have gone beyond their remit," he said.

"We've seen this happen before with other instances of high-profile incidents and people get caught — and they get caught because we have the systems in place to be able to detect this type of activity."

SASMOA chief industrial officer Bernadette Mulholland says the public needs to have confidence in the integrity of the system. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

South Australian Salaried Medical Officers Association chief industrial officer Bernadette Mulholland said such cases eroded trust in the system.

"It does create some significant concern when we hear these sorts of things may be happening," she said.

"It's really important that these records are to remain confidential, and the only people who should be looking at those records are people providing clinical care or it's necessary for the patient care.

"We want to have confidence in our health system."

World.title: Norway set to file complaint over Trump's push to overturn red card
World.content:
US President Donald Trump's role in clearing Folarin Balogun from a mandatory one-game ban at the World Cup is set to provoke a formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators.

The Norway soccer federation said its board of directors will consider filing the complaint at its next meeting, likely on August 6.

"We need our leader in FIFA to say that this was an error," Norwegian federation president Lise Klaveness told The Times in an interview.

After Trump called FIFA president Gianni Infantino, a one-game ban for Balogun's red-card tackle against Bosnia-Herzegovina was deferred so he could play against Belgium with a quarterfinals place at stake.

Belgium beat the US 4-1 after a chaotic 36 hours at the World Cup. The Belgium players were seemingly fired up by one of the greatest controversies in tournament history.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino (left) with Crown Prince Haakon of Norway and Football Association of Norway president Lise Klaveness. (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Trump called the referee's red card for Balogun after video review a "horrible" call and took credit for getting FIFA to review what should routinely have been a one-game ban.

"We all know that this verdict was influenced from external forces and did not have the proper process," Klaveness said of the FIFA ruling that was unprecedented in the past 60 years at World Cups.

"When you bend a rule like this, you're on a slippery slope that will put the whole game at risk," said the former Women's World Cup player for Norway, who is an elected member of European soccer body UEFA's executive committee.

Klaveness is a lawyer and judge who has positioned the Norwegian federation as a conscience in world soccer since her election in 2022.

"It is a worry for the game when you compromise fundamental rules of the game," she said about not enforcing Balogun's ban.

Norway previously joined a London-based NGO's complaint to the FIFA ethics committee alleging Infantino breached a statutory duty of political neutrality, including by creating a peace prize to award to Trump at the World Cup draw in December.

EU politicians launch bid to investigate FIFA boss A group of European politicians launches a bid to begin an investigation into how and why a red card for an American football star was overturned at the World Cup.

The close personal and political ties between Trump and Infantino include the US president believing the soccer official could be a good pick as next secretary general of the United Nations, the New York Post reported this week.

The human rights NGO, FairSquare, also has filed an ethics complaint about the Balogun incident to the International Olympic Committee, where Infantino is an elected member, about breaching its rules on political neutrality.

FIFA and the IOC rarely acknowledge or provide updates on potential cases before their ethics bodies.

The independence of FIFA's process to handle complaints alleging unethical conduct has been questioned since the lead investigator and judge both were replaced in 2017, in the second year of Infantino's presidency.

FIFA has yet to publish documents explaining how its disciplinary judges reached verdicts about Balogun or other World Cup players.

World.title: MotoGP to rev up motorcycle culture and pilgrimages to City of Churches
World.content:
The arrival of the Tour Down Under to Adelaide in 1999 inspired a significant uptick in Lycra-wearing cyclists in and around Adelaide, a trend that continued well into the late 2010s.

But with MotoGP landing in the City of Churches from 2027, and a Superbike World Championship round in Tailem Bend from 2028, it poses the question: Will this result in thousands of high-performance sport bikes whizzing around our roads?

Noah Orozgani works in sales at family business Moto Adelaide and says retailers believe the MotoGP is a major coup for the state.

"Like the time we had a big name like [MotoGP rider] Jack Miller come and ride for the Australian Superbikes," he says.

"There was big crowd there at Tailem Bend, the racetrack and people just went there to watch Jack Miller.

" Now there will be 20-something potential world champions riding through the streets of Adelaide. "

He says the MotoGP bikes and their riders are "out of this world" in terms of their performance and the excitement would rub off on spectators of all ages, which would in turn be good for dealerships and service centres.

Popular Australian MotoGP rider Jack Miller was rolled out for the SA government's February announcement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"The fan base is not like anything else. They get really riled up, like footy fans," he says.

"People will fly in to be a part of it, it will be huge, and getting to watch them for real, sales will go berserk.

"People are doing 360 kilometres per hour, and it just gives you that buzz, and they'll go: 'Oh yeah, I've got a bike at home, I'll go riding, and then the bike's not good enough, I need an upgrade, or a service.'"

Revving up hype

Motorcycle Alliance of South Australia chairman Heath Norris says it's likely a lot more motorcycles will be brought out of people's sheds.

"It always brings a bit of hype along with it, this sort of thing," he says.

He says Adelaide already has a strong motorcycle culture, with "great roads, great scenery and great destinations", as well as flagship charity events, like the Motorcycle Riders' Association of SA Toy Run.

Heath Norris during the 2025 charity toy run. (Supplied: Heath Norris)

That being said, he points out there is a difference between the high-performance sport bikes, or "crotch rockets" developed into superbikes, and cruiser bikes like Harley-Davidsons.

"But we're all bike enthusiasts at the end of the day," Mr Norris says.

The South Australian government is banking on strong interest in the MotoGP to warrant expenditure forecast by the former F1 Grand Prix track designer to be more than $100m to adapt the racecourse alone.

It is also facing strong and ongoing public criticism over the removal of Parklands trees that will be required to adjust the track for the MotoGP.

Banking on a big impact

A spokesperson says the 2025 MotoGP event at Phillip Island delivered an average of "$217 million in economic impact for local economies through "global exposure combined with tourism and hospitality".

Estimates MotoGP remodel could cost $100m Adelaide Street Circuit designer Bob Barnard estimates it could cost more than $100 million to remodel the track for the MotoGP.

"MotoGP has a global fan base of more than 639 million people, with a record 3.6 million attendees in races in 2025 and TV audiences up 9 per cent over the past year," he says.

The spokesperson says it is a "major global sporting property with an established national and international audience".

"South Australians will no doubt embrace motorcycle racing with the same enthusiasm we've embraced cycling, Supercars, golf and the arts, among many others."

A world first

While Victoria's Phillip Island Grand Prix racecourse is regarded as among the best worldwide, enthusiasts have said the location had limits when it came to accessibility.

The Adelaide MotoGP street circuit will be in the city's east parklands and Victoria Park. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

A street circuit like Adelaide, the world's first, was expected to draw significant international visitors, and its timing alongside the Supercars Championship Adelaide Grand Final would further bolster attention.

Mr Orozgani points out that every year there was a huge contingent of people who would ride bikes over to Phillip Island via the Great Ocean Road to watch the MotoGP.

"Religiously, they went to Melbourne to watch the races and come back," Mr Orozgani says.

Describing the end of that annual event as a "downside" to the MotoGP coming to SA, he adds it may mean people interstate will ride their bikes to Adelaide instead.

The Phillip Island GP track is considered among the best of its kind in the world. (Supplied: Ading Attamimi)

Raising awareness

Mr Norris hopes an increased profile through motorcycle racing will improve road awareness among other road users, pointing out that Adelaide drivers are not always willing to share the road.

Some Adelaide drivers struggle to accommodate road cyclists as well, particularly those who legally ride two abreast. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"I've ridden in Queensland, and people get out of your way when they see you coming up behind," he says.

" It's just that some people are quite arrogant here. They think that lane filtering is illegal, for example. "

Lane filtering is when a motorcycle rider edges between two lanes of stationary traffic on the same side of the road, or traffic moving at 30km/h or less in the same direction, which is a legal and practical activity to ease congestion.

"A lot of people here are oblivious to motorcycles," Mr Norris says.

Dealerships are expecting the MotoGP to boost Adelaide interest in motorcycles. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Asked if SAPOL was expecting more high-performance sport bikes on the roads as a result of the MotoGP, Officer in Charge of Traffic Services Branch Superintendent Shane Johns says it is committed to improving road safety for all road users.

"Major events can result in increased traffic volumes, including more motorcycles on our roads," he says.

"SAPOL routinely plans for these events with an appropriate policing response, which includes targeted road safety operations where required.

"SAPOL encourages all motorcyclists to ride within the speed limit, to the conditions, and to make responsible decisions on the road."

A motorcyclist caught at 200 kilometres per hour in an 80km/h zone in the Adelaide Hills during 2015. (Supplied: SA Police)

World.title: Why Waratahs 'trust each other' to deliver in grand final against Drua
World.content:
Confidence can sometimes be mistaken for arrogance, but NSW Waratahs captain Emily Chancellor knows how to distinguish between the two.

Therefore, it is no surprise the Waratahs took pride in their 33-22 win over the Western Force in the Super Rugby Women's semifinals, but refused to get carried away with their performance.

"We got out on the field in that semifinal and there was just this air of clarity around the group," Chancellor told ABC Sport.

"It wasn't arrogance. It was just this feeling of we know what to do and we know how to do it, so let's just go out and execute."

As they prepare to face Fijian Drua in Saturday's grand final in Ba, Fiji, the Waratahs have reason to be in a confident mood.

Last Saturday against the Force in Perth, the defending champions produced arguably the best 40 minutes of rugby from any side this season.

They ran in four tries during the first half and led 26-0 before the Force were able to score their first points.

The Force, who earned hosting rights by finishing above the Waratahs on the standings, clawed back some ground on the scoreboard in the second half.

But the result was never in doubt.

"We know we've got firepower out wide. We know we've got electric backs," Chancellor said.

"We've got a really strong, physical forward pack that has been quite consistent across the last few years.

"We know the forwards are doing a really good job of going direct and then it's up to the backs to do what they do best."

Waiaria Ellis was superb for the Waratahs in their semifinal win over the Force. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

It was a return to form for the Waratahs, who entered the play-offs in third place.

They dropped their final two regular-season matches against the Force (28-21) and the Queensland Reds (26-19).

The loss to the Force was the first time they had been defeated by an Australian opponent in Super Rugby Women's history.

But sudden-death rugby has become second nature to the Waratahs, who have only missed one grand final among the seven contested in the competition.

The six-time winners were rewarded for taking a punt on an untried halves pairing, Tia Hinds and Waiaria Ellis, with the selection move proving to be a masterstroke.

Hinds, an Australian sevens star making her Waratahs debut, was a revelation at scrum half, scoring two tries when she caught the Force's ruck defence napping.

She combined brilliantly with 18-year-old Wallaroos sensation Ellis, who helped drive the Waratahs' attack in her first start at fly half this season after switching from fullback.

"They (Hinds and Ellis) backed themselves," said Chancellor, who has played almost 40 Tests for the Wallaroos.

"Tia, being an incredible reader of space, took her own opportunities, and Baba (Ellis) did a really good job of being calm and collected.

"She had a really sound knowledge of our game plan and was just able to deliver and execute what she saw in front of her."

Tahs face stern test

The Drua, who have won two Super Rugby Women's championships, were impressive in their 31-5 victory over the Reds in the first semifinal in Lautoka last Saturday.

They deservedly finished the regular season on top of the standings with a 3-1 win-loss record.

But their one defeat came at the hands of the Waratahs, who triumphed 42-29 at Leichhardt Oval in the opening round.

The Waratahs defeated the Drua when they played in the opening round of the regular season. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"Fiji would probably be disappointed that it's us in the final," Chancellor said.

"We're probably the hardest ones for them to beat, in the same way they're the hardest ones for us to beat. They've been playing some really great rugby.

"They play a style that is hard to defend against, but in the same breath it creates a lot of opportunity because they do play a high-risk, high-reward version of rugby.

"So if we can withstand some pressure and stay disciplined, I believe we have an attacking game that will be hard to contain."

Chancellor's faith in her Waratahs teammates is not misplaced, as it is built on a key trait the entire squad shares: confidence.

"We're a squad who knows how to play big games," she said.

"The Waratahs are a team that knows how to win in big moments. We know how to win; we know how to perform under these pressure moments.

"We take a lot of confidence because we trust each other to do our own jobs."

World.title: Out of necessity is borne a unique and wholly Scottish opening ceremony
World.content:
The Glasgow Commonwealth Games was more or less forced inside.

The shortened preparation time meant it was simply easier to host most events in halls and exhibition centres that already existed, and a solid roof removes the many variables that Scotland's weather can introduce to proceedings.

It meant the opening ceremony, for the first time in history, would be held in an arena rather than a stadium. And what a blessing it turned out to be.

Australia emerged late in the athletes' parade, which was divided by regions as well as nations. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

If you've ever witnessed a rock band or pop star playing before a major football game you'll know the energy is very rarely on point.

It's just too far, the noise dissipates, and charismatic frontmen and global superstars are reduced to little more than carnival barkers, pleading with a distracted crowd to "put your hands up. Please".

On Thursday night in Glasgow the crowd filed in as the perfect weather turned cool for the first time this week. Local DJ Hu Sane and radio presenters kept the crowd relatively entertained with the sort of pre-show antics you'd expect from a warm-up act.

The opening skit with cycling great Sir Chris Hoy, former Doctor Who star Sylvester McCoy and actor Greg McHugh served its purpose of delivering a few knowing chuckles and delivering King Charles III and Queen Camilla in a TARDIS.

King Charles III's arrival was the sort of thing we've come to expect from opening ceremonies. The rest of the show wasn't. (AP: Manish Swarup)

But from the opening strains of synth-heavy electro-folk band Valtos it was clear this ceremony would feel different.

As the athletes entered the arena, messages from local kids or well-meaning and poorly read adults, were projected on the screens wrapping around the upper decks.

"I hope you win the game, good luck best wishes from Gulalai" "Good luck! I hope you enjoy Glasgow — our green place, you can do this!" "Have fun you can do it. I hope you do well be brave." "Good luck. Believe in yourself be proud of yourself. From Leah."

Nina Kennedy and Tim Hodge led the team into the arena. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Scotland is a nation that prides itself on being small but mighty. Fittingly, the smaller the team the larger the cheer during the parade, with the loudest reserved for St Lucia.

The tiny Caribbean nation brought just three athletes to Glasgow and only the chef de mission marched. But she was welcomed like a Glaswegian local.

Then came the main attraction.

When in doubt, pipe. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Scotland's athletes danced their way to their seats accompanied by rapturous applause from the 14,000-strong crowd, before a cameo by Nessie, pipers and Outlander's Sam Heughan.

Then those supporters briefly turned into the stars of the show.

The same crowd that gleefully welcomed the current British monarch to Glasgow an hour earlier joined pipers and drummers in a stirring, reverberative rendition of Flower of Scotland, the national anthem about King of the Scots Robert the Bruce driving King Edward II's army back at the Battle of Bannockburn.

The pipes were indeed calling. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Fiji's noqu masu, New Zealand's haka, Samoa's siva tau (performed by the team as they emerged for the parade) can crack stone hearts and soak eyes that don't cry at funerals.

This was one of those moments.

The sounds of the pipes bouncing off the walls, the power of the drums rattling through the seats and the choral sensation cascading from the upper decks all ended up in the same place: deep in the bones of all those in attendance.

The size, shape and set-up of the venue made it feel like a more intimate performance than the sort of extravaganza intended for hundreds of millions of people to watch on TV.

There was a theme of gardens and nature throughout the ceremony. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

It was enough to make everyone in the arena want to be Scottish, but most of all Commonwealth Sport president Donald Rukare.

"It's good to be back," he said.

The thanks to the 2014 hosts and ensuing elation from the Scottish crowd came with an undertone of side-eye to the slack left by Victoria's 2023 rug-pull.

Both Scotland and Australia pride themselves on punching above their weight, taking things in stride with good humour and getting on with the job.

There was a party atmosphere for the athletes' parade. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

But only one of those countries is putting on these Games. And there does seem to be a genuine feeling of pride in Glasgow for stepping into a tough situation, albeit with help from a few hundred million dollars from Victorian taxpayers.

During his speech, Rukare said he hoped the crowd would indulge him sporting a Wallace tartan kilt, re-imagined in the colours of his native Uganda.

Indulge him? Saltires flew with the sort of fervour usually reserved for the athletes who will take centre stage for the next 10 days.

By the time King Charles officially declared the Games open, the whole event turned into a concert courtesy of Callum Beattie, Tom Walker and KT Tunstall.

The lead-up to these Games has at times shown the hallmarks of a major global event pulled together under an intense time crunch.

But the opening ceremony, aside perhaps from a few eisteddfod-level costumes, overcame that with a passion and spirit that was purely Scotland.

Rukare has spoken about making the Games fit for purpose, even if that means getting smaller in some ways, to remain relevant.

After this opening it's hard to imagine going back.

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share it with us.

World.title: Stage winner almost hits overzealous fan in gruelling Tour de France climb
World.content:
Ecuadorian rider Richard Carapaz timed his attack perfectly in the final climb to win the 18th stage of the Tour de France, while also surviving a near miss with a spectator.

It was the 33-year-old Carapaz's first stage win at this year's race and second overall. Leader Tadej Pogačar did not chase him down because Carapaz is not considered a threat to win the Tour and is in 10th spot.

"This is a wonderful victory," Carapaz said.

"I dedicate it to my family."

After moving ahead about 3 kilometres from the summit, Carapaz raced clear. He patted each side of his head as he approached the finish line, and was 45 seconds ahead of Swiss rider Mauro Schmid and American Matteo Jorgenson.

"It's been a special day. It took a lot of hard work," said Carapaz, who failed to win with a similar breakaway earlier in this year's race.

"This is the most rewarding thing for me, knowing that the work I put in has paid off."

Pogačar is chasing a third straight Tour title and fifth overall. The Slovenian star rolled over the line in a large group containing his closest rival, Remco Evenepoel, and Pogačar's UAE Emirates XRG teammate, Isaac Del Toro.

There was no change overall as Pogačar maintained his lead of 4 minutes, 32 seconds over the Belgian time trial star Evenepoel, the winner of two stages at this year's race, and 6:51 over the 22-year-old Mexican Del Toro in third overall.

The overnight stage was the first of three straight days of Alpine climbs.

The 185km trek featured an early Category 1 climb — the second-hardest category — up Côte d'Engins, before ending with a Category 1 ascent to the Orcières-Merlette ski station.

After going over Engins, Jorgenson was in a small group at the front. They were then joined by Carapaz, with Pogačar's yellow jersey group clearly hanging back.

"I think nobody would really commit," said Pogačar, who has won four stages at this year's race.

Carapaz's stage could have ended when he had a near miss with a fan standing in the road, but he swerved around him just in time.

Heading into the final climb up Orcières-Merlette, Jorgenson and Schmid could not respond when Carapaz, who won the 2019 Giro d'Italia, attacked.

"This final climb was tough and suited my strengths well," said Carapaz, whose other Tour stage win came in 2024.

"This was a hard-fought victory, but just as tough as the first one. It gets harder every year to win here."

The 19th stage ends with a HC climb (the hardest category) up L'Alpe d'Huez, an iconic Tour climb and among the most famed in cycling.

The 20th and penultimate stage is brutal and could be epic. It features three HC climbs — Col de la Croix de Fer, Col du Galibier and Col de Sarenne — and one Category 1 climb up Col du Télégraphe, before a hilly finish to L'Alpe d'Huez.

The race ends on the Champs-Élysées in Paris on Sunday night AEST.
